sections.title: Water reactions: evidence for an alkali-metal family
paragraphs: Lithium, sodium and potassium are Group 1 metals. In reactions with cold water they produce hydrogen gas and the corresponding metal hydroxide. The hydroxide dissolves to give an alkaline solution. These shared products and similar reaction patterns support treating the elements as a chemical family; similar appearance alone is weaker evidence.

The general word equation is alkali metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen. For sodium, the balanced symbol equation is 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂. The two water molecules supply four hydrogen atoms: two remain in the hydroxide and two form one hydrogen molecule. Potassium follows the same pattern: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂.

Fizzing is an observation that gas is produced; identifying that gas as hydrogen is a further conclusion supported by appropriate test evidence. A suitable indicator can show that the resulting solution is alkaline, but indicator colour must be interpreted using the named indicator. Phenolphthalein changes from colourless to pink in an alkaline solution.

Compare the shared type of reaction separately from how vigorously each metal reacts. This is an explanation of evidence from a supervised demonstration, not instructions to perform one. These metals and the alkaline products can cause harm; any demonstration requires the institution’s trained staff and safety procedures. Hydrogen is not an alkali metal even though it is placed above Group 1 in many periodic tables.

example.question: A question states that lithium, sodium and potassium each produce hydrogen and an alkaline solution with water. Explain how this supports their classification as a family.
steps: Identify the shared gas product as hydrogen.
Identify the solution products as the corresponding metal hydroxides.
Connect the same reaction pattern and product types to similar chemical behaviour.
example.explanation: The evidence is chemical similarity. It does not imply identical reaction rates or the same hydroxide compound.

commonMistakes: Calling hydrogen a metal hydroxide or an alkali metal.
Writing Na + H₂O → NaOH + H₂ without balancing it.
Treating fizzing alone as conclusive identification of hydrogen.

sections.title: Air and water: comparing lithium, sodium and potassium
paragraphs: Typical supervised demonstrations show increasing reactivity in the order lithium < sodium < potassium. With comparable small samples in cold water, lithium usually fizzes relatively gently; sodium reacts more vigorously and may melt into a moving ball because heat is released. Potassium usually reacts still more vigorously and may ignite, giving a lilac flame. These observations are examples of typical behaviour, not guaranteed outcomes for every sample.

Freshly exposed surfaces are silvery, but reaction with substances in air produces a dull surface layer. Sodium and potassium usually tarnish faster than lithium under comparable conditions. Faster surface change provides further evidence for increasing reactivity down Group 1. Air contains oxygen and water vapour, so do not assume every surface layer is a single simple oxide.

An observation is what is seen, such as fizzing, movement or loss of shine. A reactivity ranking is an interpretation of a pattern across the metals. More vigorous reaction can support that ranking, but reaction time alone is a poor comparison when sample mass, exposed surface or water temperature differs. A large lithium sample and a tiny potassium sample do not provide a controlled test of the group trend.

The shared water-reaction products identify family similarities; the different vigour and air-reaction rates distinguish positions within the family. A defensible answer names the observation, states the order and connects the two. No trial has been performed for these notes, and the examples are not measured data.

example.question: A written demonstration report describes gentle lithium fizzing, faster sodium reaction and still more vigorous potassium reaction under comparable conditions. State the trend and give one limitation of the evidence.
steps: State that reactivity increases from lithium to sodium to potassium.
Use the reported increase in vigour as the supporting observation.
Explain that unequal surface area, sample size or temperature could weaken a comparison; the report does not give a numerical rate.
example.explanation: The qualitative report supports the usual ordering. It does not establish exact rate ratios, and flame absence would not by itself reverse the ranking.

commonMistakes: Ranking the metals by atomic mass without referring to reaction evidence.
Claiming sodium always melts or potassium always ignites.
Assuming that every Group 1 air-reaction product has the formula M₂O.

sections.title: Predicting another alkali metal without inventing results
paragraphs: Use a periodic-table position to extend a known group pattern. Rubidium lies below potassium in Group 1, so it is expected to react more vigorously with water under comparable conditions. Like the other alkali metals, it forms a +1 ion and its water-reaction products are rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen. The predicted reaction pattern is 2Rb + 2H₂O → 2RbOH + H₂.

Separate properties shared by the family from trends down the family. Forming a +1 ion and producing a hydroxide with water are family patterns. Increasing reactivity down the group is a directional trend. Softer metals and generally lower melting points are familiar Group 1 patterns, but a prediction must be limited to what the evidence or stated trend supports.

A trend does not provide an exact reaction time, temperature, flame colour or numerical melting point. It also does not mean that every physical property changes smoothly: density, for example, is not a simple steadily increasing sequence across lithium, sodium and potassium. Use supplied data when a question asks for a numerical estimate, and label an extrapolation as a prediction rather than a measured result.

Do not propose an unsupervised water test of a more reactive metal to check the prediction. The learning task is to reason from reliable evidence and periodic position. Prediction remains distinct from experimental verification.

example.question: Rubidium is below potassium in Group 1. Predict its products with water and relative reactivity. Can the group trend give an exact time for a sample to disappear?
steps: Predict rubidium hydroxide and hydrogen.
Predict greater reactivity than potassium under comparable conditions.
Reject an exact disappearance time: sample size, conditions and numerical rate data are unspecified.
example.explanation: Two qualitative predictions are justified by the family pattern and direction of the reactivity trend. No invented measurement is needed.

commonMistakes: Predicting Rb²⁺ because rubidium is lower in the group.
Claiming that every physical property increases down Group 1.
Presenting a guessed time or flame colour as an observed result.

sections.title: Why reactivity increases down Group 1 — Paper 2C
paragraphs: The electronic configurations of lithium, sodium and potassium are 2,1; 2,8,1; and 2,8,8,1. Each has one electron in its outer shell. A Group 1 metal atom forms a +1 ion by losing that electron. In an oxidation half-equation this is M → M⁺ + e⁻. It does not gain an electron or lose an entire outer shell of many electrons.

Down Group 1, atoms have additional occupied electron shells. The outer electron is farther from the nucleus, and more inner electrons shield it from nuclear attraction. Although the nucleus has more protons, the combined increase in distance and shielding makes the outer electron easier to remove. Less energy is needed to remove that first electron.

Connect the electronic explanation to the chemical trend: easier loss of the outer electron supports greater reactivity down the group in these reactions. Merely saying “there are more shells” misses the link through weaker attraction and easier electron loss. The number of outer electrons stays one; it is the number of occupied shells and the attraction experienced by that electron that change.

Pearson marks this particular explanation as 2.4C, applying to Paper 2C only in the saved Issue 3 specification. The observable trends and predictions in 2.1–2.3 apply to both 1C and 2C. Electronic reasoning explains the trend; it does not determine an exact demonstration rate from configuration alone.

example.question: Why does potassium react more vigorously with water than sodium? Explain using their electronic configurations.
steps: Both atoms have one outer electron: sodium 2,8,1 and potassium 2,8,8,1.
Potassium has an additional occupied shell, so its outer electron is farther from the nucleus and more shielded.
The outer electron is less strongly attracted and is lost more easily, supporting potassium’s greater reactivity.
example.explanation: The chain is configuration → distance and shielding → easier electron loss → greater reactivity. Potassium’s larger positive nuclear charge alone would not explain the observed direction.

commonMistakes: Saying potassium has more outer electrons than sodium.
Claiming nuclear charge decreases down the group.
Using “it gains one electron” as the alkali-metal explanation.

sections.title: Chlorine, bromine and iodine: colours and states
paragraphs: Pearson’s Group 7 halogens are the elements labelled Group 17 in the modern 1–18 periodic table. Chlorine, bromine and iodine are non-metals whose elemental molecules are Cl₂, Br₂ and I₂. A chlorine molecule, Cl₂, is different from a chloride ion, Cl⁻; likewise bromine and iodine are distinct from bromide and iodide ions.

At about 20°C and ordinary atmospheric pressure, chlorine is a yellow-green gas, bromine a red-brown liquid, and iodine a grey-black, shiny crystalline solid. Give both the colour and the state when describing each element. These descriptions concern the elemental substances, not their ions in salts.

Iodine vapour is purple. That does not make the room-temperature solid purple: the description depends on the state being observed. Iodine can produce vapour from a solid, but it also has a melting point and can exist as a liquid under suitable conditions. Avoid the absolute claim that iodine never melts.

Across chlorine, bromine and iodine, the appearance becomes darker and melting and boiling points increase. At the same room temperature their states consequently change from gas to liquid to solid. Colour alone does not establish a reaction or quantify chemical reactivity. These are reference descriptions, not observations from an experiment performed for this site.

example.question: Three elemental samples at 20°C are described as a yellow-green gas, a red-brown liquid and a grey-black solid. Identify them. Which description applies to iodine vapour?
steps: Yellow-green gas: chlorine, Cl₂.
Red-brown liquid: bromine, Br₂.
Grey-black solid: iodine, I₂; its vapour is purple.
example.explanation: Pair each element with its state as well as colour. Iodide ions in a salt are not the same substance as elemental iodine.

commonMistakes: Calling solid iodine purple because its vapour is purple.
Writing Cl⁻ as the formula of elemental chlorine.
Describing bromine as a room-temperature gas because it gives off vapour.

sections.title: Predicting physical properties from halogen data
paragraphs: Compare numerical melting and boiling points to establish the physical trend. Rounded reference values in °C are chlorine −101.5 / −34.04, bromine −7.2 / 58.8, and iodine 113.7 / 184.4, written as melting / boiling point. Both sets increase in that order. The values come from RSC reference data; they are not measurements made for this site.

At a stated pressure, a temperature below the melting point normally places a pure substance in the solid region; a temperature between its melting and boiling points places it in the liquid region; and a temperature above its boiling point places it in the gas region. At a transition temperature, two phases can coexist during the change. At 20°C chlorine is above its boiling point, bromine is between its two transition points, and iodine is below its melting point.

The simple molecular explanation connects larger, more polarizable molecules to stronger intermolecular attractions down this sequence. More energy is required to separate molecules, so melting and boiling points rise. Changing state does not require breaking the covalent bond inside each X₂ molecule. Do not confuse intermolecular attraction with that internal covalent bond.

Use the established trend to make a limited prediction for another halogen. A halogen above chlorine is expected to have lower melting and boiling points; because chlorine’s boiling point is already below 20°C, a lower boiling point supports a gas prediction at 20°C. A halogen below iodine is expected to have higher transition temperatures and to be solid at 20°C in this simple extrapolation. Exact values and an exact colour cannot be calculated from group position alone; check supplied data and label extrapolations as predictions.

Melting and boiling describe physical changes. Increasing transition temperatures does not prove increasing chemical reactivity. Displacement reactions and their electronic explanation are covered separately below. The state example below is a written reasoning exercise, not advice to heat a halogen sample.

example.question: Using iodine’s reference melting point of 113.7°C and boiling point of 184.4°C, predict its stable bulk state at 120°C at ordinary atmospheric pressure. Explain why purple vapour does not mean iodine cannot be liquid.
steps: Compare the temperature: 113.7 < 120 < 184.4.
It is above the melting point and below the boiling point, so the stable bulk phase is liquid.
Vapour can exist above a liquid or solid; seeing vapour alone does not establish the bulk sample’s state.
example.explanation: The supplied transition temperatures and pressure determine the phase prediction. The calculation does not describe a performed experiment.

commonMistakes: Assuming a larger halogen always has greater chemical reactivity because its boiling point is higher.
Saying boiling breaks the covalent bond inside every X₂ molecule.
Inventing an exact melting point or colour for an unfamiliar halogen from its group position alone.

sections.title: Halogen displacement: predict the product, not just a colour
paragraphs: In these aqueous displacement reactions, a more reactive halogen converts the halide ions of a less reactive halogen into that elemental halogen. Chlorine molecules can react with bromide or iodide ions; bromine molecules can react with iodide ions. Chlorine is therefore more reactive than bromine, which is more reactive than iodine in this comparison: chlorine > bromine > iodine.

Keep the species distinct. In chlorine plus potassium bromide solution, the starting reactive species are Cl₂ molecules and Br⁻ ions. The products are Cl⁻ ions and Br₂ molecules. Potassium ions remain in solution as spectator ions. Saying “chlorine displaces bromide to form bromine” identifies the initial ion and final element; saying “chlorine ions displace bromine ions” mixes up the reactants.

Bromine does not displace chloride, and iodine does not displace chloride or bromide under the usual aqueous comparison conditions. A halogen mixed with its own halide produces no net displacement of one element by another. These negative outcomes constrain the ranking. “No displacement” does not mean “no colour”: the original halogen can still colour the mixture.

The matrix shows predicted outcomes, not measured results. Read each row as the added elemental halogen and each column as the halide already in the solution. A Br₂ or I₂ product is the newly formed element, while the added more reactive halogen becomes its own halide ion. Other reactions or equilibria are not ruled out by a no-displacement entry.

diagram.alt: Predicted matrix: chlorine forms bromine from bromide and iodine from iodide; bromine forms iodine from iodide; other pairs show no displacement.
diagram.caption: Original schematic of predicted aqueous displacement outcomes. It does not represent a performed experiment or exact observed colours.

example.question: A supplied results table shows chlorine displacing bromide and iodide, while bromine displaces iodide but not chloride. Rank the three halogens and predict iodine with bromide.
steps: Chlorine displaces both other halides, so it is the most reactive of the three.
Bromine displaces iodide but not chloride, placing it between chlorine and iodine.
The order is chlorine > bromine > iodine; iodine does not displace bromide in this comparison.
example.explanation: The ranking follows the stated positive and negative displacement evidence. The hypothetical table is not a trial performed for this site.

commonMistakes: Treating Cl₂ and Cl⁻ as interchangeable reactants.
Calling the incoming potassium ion the displaced species.
Assuming no displacement means the liquid must be colourless.

sections.title: Balance displacement equations by atoms and charge
paragraphs: For chlorine reacting with potassium bromide solution, a balanced complete equation is Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂. The net ionic equation removes unchanged K⁺ spectator ions: Cl₂ + 2Br⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + Br₂. There are two chlorine and two bromine atoms on each side, and the total charge is −2 on each side.

The other predicted positive outcomes are Cl₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Cl⁻ + I₂ and Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂. Each starts with a neutral diatomic halogen and two negative halide ions, and produces two halide ions plus one neutral diatomic halogen. Writing just one iodide ion would fail atom balance.

Electron transfer explains the ionic form. For chlorine and bromide: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ is reduction because chlorine gains electrons; 2Br⁻ → Br₂ + 2e⁻ is oxidation because bromide loses electrons. Adding the half-equations cancels the electrons and gives the net ionic equation. The chlorine molecules act as the oxidizing agent in this reaction.

Check a proposed equation against the reactivity order before balancing it. Br₂ + 2Cl⁻ → 2Br⁻ + Cl₂ can be balanced on paper, but it is not the expected spontaneous displacement in the stated aqueous comparison. Atom and charge balance are necessary checks; they do not by themselves establish that a reaction occurs.

example.question: Write the net ionic equation for bromine displacing iodide. Check the atom counts and total charge.
steps: Use Br₂ and I⁻ as reactants, with Br⁻ and I₂ as products.
Balance: Br₂ + 2I⁻ → 2Br⁻ + I₂.
Both sides have two bromine and two iodine atoms; both have total charge −2.
example.explanation: The relative reactivity supports the direction. Coefficients conserve the atoms and charge without turning elemental bromine into a single Br atom.

commonMistakes: Writing I rather than I₂ for elemental iodine.
Leaving spectator K⁺ ions in a supposedly net ionic equation.
Assuming any balanced reverse equation describes an observed reaction.

sections.title: What observations can actually establish displacement?
paragraphs: An interpretation needs the known starting substances and reliable product evidence. Bromine commonly gives orange to brown solutions depending on concentration and solvent; iodine gives brown aqueous solutions and violet solutions in a suitable nonpolar solvent. Compare a reported product with a reference of the same halogen in the same solvent, rather than comparing an aqueous colour with a vapour colour.

A lighter original colour may be caused by dilution, so colour fading alone does not prove displacement. A mixture can also retain some colour from excess added halogen. If a question reports a violet nonpolar layer matching an iodine reference after bromine contacts iodide, that supports iodine formation. The reactant identities and product comparison jointly support the conclusion.

A useful supervised comparison keeps conditions and concentration comparisons consistent, separates samples to avoid contamination, uses corresponding reference colours and records positive as well as negative outcomes. Distinguish a proposed comparison from actual recorded data. For a negative outcome, fresh reagents and suitable observations matter: a degraded halogen solution can give a misleading absence of visible reaction.

The learning task here is interpreting supplied evidence, not preparing halogens or running a solvent extraction. Halogens and many extraction solvents require professional laboratory controls. No preparation recipe, exact dose or unsupervised experimental method is supplied. The original problem below states its observations as hypothetical data.

example.question: A hypothetical report says bromine solution contacted iodide solution. The nonpolar layer then matched a violet iodine reference. In a separate mixture, bromine’s original colour merely became lighter after adding chloride solution. Interpret both results.
steps: The first product comparison supports iodine formation: bromine displaces iodide.
The second colour fading could result from dilution; it does not establish chlorine formation.
The expected ranking predicts no bromine displacement of chloride; use matched references and known conditions rather than colour fading alone.
example.explanation: A product-specific comparison is stronger evidence than a change in colour intensity. Neither description is a performed trial.

commonMistakes: Using purple iodine vapour as the reference for an aqueous solution.
Treating any colour change as proof of a displacement product.
Promoting hypothetical supplied observations to real measurements.

sections.title: Why halogen reactivity decreases down the group — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Chlorine, bromine and iodine atoms each have seven electrons in their outer shell. Their shell configurations are 2,8,7; 2,8,18,7; and 2,8,18,18,7. In the displacement reactions being considered, halogen atoms gain one electron each to form −1 halide ions. For a chlorine molecule the reduction half-equation is Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻: two atoms need two electrons in total.

Down the group there are more occupied shells. An incoming electron joins a shell farther from the nucleus and experiences more shielding by inner electrons. Despite the increase in proton number, the attraction experienced by an incoming outer-shell electron is weaker in this simplified explanation. Electron gain is less readily achieved in the chlorine–bromine–iodine reactivity comparison.

Connect the mechanism to the evidence: chlorine gains electrons more readily than bromine, and bromine more readily than iodine in these displacement comparisons. Chemical reactivity therefore decreases down this sequence. Do not explain the trend by saying that lower atoms have fewer protons or fewer outer electrons; both statements are wrong.

Compare with Group 1 carefully. Increased distance and shielding make an outer electron easier to lose for alkali metals, supporting increasing Group 1 reactivity. For these halogens the important step is gaining an electron, which becomes less readily achieved down the group. The same structural changes can therefore support opposite reactivity trends.

This electronic explanation is own 2.8C, applying only to Paper 2C in the saved Issue 3 specification. Displacement evidence in 2.7 applies to both 1C and 2C. The shell model explains the qualitative trend; it does not calculate an exact reaction rate or every quantitative property of every heavier halogen.

example.question: Explain why bromine is less reactive than chlorine in the halide-displacement comparison, even though bromine has more protons.
steps: Both atoms have seven outer electrons and gain one electron per atom to form halide ions.
Bromine has more occupied shells, greater distance to the outer shell and more inner-electron shielding.
These effects reduce the attraction for an incoming outer-shell electron despite the greater proton number, making electron gain less readily achieved.
example.explanation: Give the complete causal chain and the correct electron-gain direction. A Group 1 answer about easier electron loss would not explain this halogen trend.

commonMistakes: Claiming nuclear charge decreases from chlorine to bromine.
Saying bromine has more than seven outer electrons.
Using easier electron loss to explain lower halogen reactivity.

sections.title: The four main gases in dry air
paragraphs: Dry air means the mixture with water vapour excluded. Approximate percentages by volume are nitrogen 78%, oxygen 21%, argon 0.9% and carbon dioxide 0.04%. These are rounded teaching values, not a measurement of today’s atmosphere. Carbon dioxide varies over time and place; other trace gases are also present.

Percentage by volume compares the volume of a component gas with the total mixture volume at the same temperature and pressure. In a hypothetical 1,000 cm³ dry-air sample, about 210 cm³ corresponds to oxygen. Do not interpret 21% as 21 g in every 100 g of air: mass percentage is a different quantity.

Water vapour varies with conditions, so moist-air percentages differ from dry-air percentages. The rounded values need not sum to exactly 100%; rounding and trace components account for the remaining difference. Argon is the third most abundant gas in dry air, ahead of carbon dioxide.

example.question: Estimate the oxygen volume in 1,000 cm³ of dry air. Which named gas has a larger proportion: argon or carbon dioxide?
steps: Use 21/100 × 1,000 = 210 cm³ oxygen, approximately.
Compare about 0.9% argon with about 0.04% carbon dioxide: argon is larger.
example.explanation: All volumes refer to the same conditions; the example is invented and uses rounded composition values.

commonMistakes: Including water vapour in a table labelled dry air.
Using 21% oxygen as a mass percentage.
Calling carbon dioxide the third most abundant dry-air gas.

sections.title: Removing oxygen with iron
paragraphs: A volume experiment can estimate oxygen by selectively consuming it from a measured air sample. Moist iron reacts with oxygen to form solid corrosion products. With enough iron, enough time and an airtight apparatus, the decrease in gas volume estimates the oxygen removed. Water is needed for rusting; dry iron is a poor choice for this method.

In a water-supported tube demonstration, water enters the space vacated as oxygen is removed. The remaining gas is smaller in volume. It is mostly nitrogen but also contains argon and other gases, so it is not pure nitrogen. Removing oxygen does not turn nitrogen into water or make every gas disappear.

Excess iron means enough is available to consume the oxygen; it does not mean all the iron must react. A stable final gas volume is evidence of an endpoint, provided the apparatus is airtight and conditions are comparable. These notes explain a school investigation; no experiment has been performed for the site.

example.question: A hypothetical sealed sample falls from 100 cm³ to 80 cm³ after complete oxygen removal. Is the remaining 80 cm³ pure nitrogen?
steps: The decrease is 20 cm³, so this sample suggests approximately 20% oxygen.
Reject pure nitrogen: argon and other unreacted gases remain.
example.explanation: An approximate experimental estimate need not equal the rounded reference value exactly.

commonMistakes: Expecting the whole iron sample to disappear.
Calling the remaining gas pure nitrogen.
Treating dry iron or a leaking apparatus as a reliable oxygen-removal method.

sections.title: The same volume principle with a non-metal
paragraphs: A suitable non-metal can also remove oxygen from air by reaction. In a teacher-controlled phosphorus demonstration, oxygen is consumed to form phosphorus oxide. Once products have been removed from the measured gas phase and the apparatus has cooled, the gas-volume decrease can be compared with the initial air volume.

For phosphorus represented as P₄, a model equation is P₄ + 5O₂ → P₄O₁₀. It conserves four phosphorus atoms and ten oxygen atoms on each side. P₂O₅ is an empirical formula for the same atomic ratio; it must not simply replace P₄O₁₀ in this equation without rebalancing.

Combustion heats gas and can introduce temporary changes in volume or pressure. Measuring while hot confuses thermal expansion with gas consumption. Use the same comparison principle as the iron method, and state excess reactant, complete oxygen removal and comparable temperature/pressure assumptions. Phosphorus handling belongs to a controlled school demonstration, not a home investigation.

example.question: Why should a teacher’s phosphorus demonstration cool before the final air volume is compared with the initial volume?
steps: Reaction heat changes gas volume even without changing the amount of gas.
Cooling to the initial temperature makes the decrease a better measure of oxygen consumed, with comparable pressure.
example.explanation: A hot final reading would mix a chemical change with a physical expansion effect.

commonMistakes: Calling a hot gas-volume change a direct oxygen percentage.
Replacing P₄O₁₀ with P₂O₅ without rebalancing.
Assuming that any non-metal removes only oxygen under every condition.

sections.title: Use the whole initial air volume
paragraphs: Use oxygen percentage ≈ (initial total air volume − final total gas volume) ÷ initial total air volume × 100. The initial total includes all connected gas spaces, not only a syringe reading. Solid and liquid volumes are not additional air volumes; use the actual gas-containing space given in the question.

Original hypothetical example: a flask holds 60 cm³ of air, a connecting tube 5 cm³, and a syringe initially 35 cm³. Initial air volume is 60 + 5 + 35 = 100 cm³. After complete removal and return to the same temperature and pressure, the syringe reads 14 cm³. Final total is 60 + 5 + 14 = 79 cm³; the decrease is 21 cm³ and the estimate is 21%.

The fixed flask and tube volumes cancel in the subtraction but still belong in the denominator. Dividing 21 by the initial syringe reading 35 would give 60%, an incorrect estimate for the whole connected sample. This is a model exercise, not measured data or a copied past-paper task.

example.question: A hypothetical apparatus has fixed gas spaces totalling 90 cm³. Its syringe changes from 30 to 6 cm³ at comparable conditions. Calculate the oxygen percentage.
steps: Initial total = 90 + 30 = 120 cm³.
Gas removed = 30 − 6 = 24 cm³.
example.explanation: The syringe difference gives the removed volume, but the original total air volume gives the denominator.

commonMistakes: Dividing only by the syringe volume.
Adding solid iron or liquid water volume as air.
Using final volume instead of initial volume in the denominator.

diagram.alt: Invented connected-air example: fixed gas spaces 65 cubic centimetres; syringe 35 initially and 14 finally; total changes 100 to 79, giving 21 percent.
diagram.caption: Original calculation schematic, not measured data or an apparatus construction plan. Fixed gas spaces remain in the initial denominator.

sections.title: Reviewing an oxygen-measurement plan
paragraphs: A school plan should specify a known initial gas volume, excess moist iron, an airtight connection and enough time for the gas volume to stop changing. Record readings with units and compare initial and final values at matching temperature and pressure. Repeat runs with fresh samples to assess consistency; do not invent results to force a value of 21%.

Read tube or syringe scales consistently and avoid parallax. A gas-column length is proportional to volume only where the tube’s cross-sectional area is constant. A rounded tube end or changing diameter can invalidate a simple length ratio; use calibrated gas volumes when that geometry matters. Equal water levels, where applicable, help match the gas pressure to outside pressure.

Insufficient iron or stopping before completion removes too little oxygen and tends to underestimate the percentage. A warmer final gas reading, at the same pressure, is larger and can also reduce the apparent decrease. Being warmer throughout is different: if both readings share the same conditions, temperature alone need not bias the fraction. Leak effects depend on when and how gas enters or escapes, so their direction cannot be asserted without details.

Wet-air composition, gas dissolution, changing conditions and limited scale resolution make this an approximate measurement. Report repeated estimates and their spread rather than claiming that agreement proves every systematic error is absent. This planning and error analysis does not certify practical competence or a completed investigation.

example.question: Two readings under matched conditions imply 19.8% and 20.2% oxygen. Calculate their mean, and explain why agreement is not proof that the apparatus was perfect.
steps: Both runs may share a systematic bias, such as incomplete oxygen removal.
The close values show consistency, not guaranteed accuracy.
example.explanation: The two percentages are invented for the calculation; no physical trial is claimed.

commonMistakes: Using a length ratio for a non-uniform tube without justification.
Calling repeatability the same as accuracy.
Claiming every leak causes an overestimate.

sections.title: Magnesium burning in oxygen
paragraphs: Combustion is a reaction with oxygen that releases energy. Magnesium gives a bright white light and forms white magnesium oxide in the intended oxygen reaction. The balanced equation is 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO: two magnesium atoms and two oxygen atoms occur on each side.

The oxide contains oxygen from the gas as well as magnesium from the metal, so the mass of the oxide exceeds the mass of the magnesium that forms it when product is retained. Brightness is an observation; formation of an oxide is a chemical interpretation supported by the reaction.

Burning in air can involve nitrogen as well as oxygen, so an actual air experiment need not produce only pure MgO. Describe the conditions stated in the question. The bright light should not be stared at in a supervised demonstration; these notes do not give an ignition procedure.

example.question: Balance Mg + O₂ → MgO and explain why the retained oxide is heavier than the magnesium used to form it.
steps: Write 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.
Oxygen atoms are added from the gas; both elements contribute to the product mass.
example.explanation: Mass is conserved when gas reactants are included; it is not created by the light.

commonMistakes: Writing MgO₂ to balance oxygen.
Ignoring the gas when explaining a mass increase.
Assuming an air experiment necessarily gives one pure product.

sections.title: Hydrogen burning: water as the product
paragraphs: Hydrogen burns in oxygen to form water and release energy: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. The hot product can be water vapour, which may condense into liquid droplets on cooling. Formation of water is the chemical change; subsequent condensation is a physical change.

The balanced equation contains four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side. Neither reactant contains carbon, so carbon dioxide is not the product of this reaction. Pure hydrogen combustion is different from burning a carbon-containing fuel.

A burning hydrogen sample can give a squeaky pop in the familiar small-scale identification test. That observation supports identification under controlled school conditions; it is not a quantitative measurement of reaction energy or evidence that every hydrogen flame looks identical.

example.question: A hot hydrogen-combustion product later forms droplets. Name the product and distinguish the two changes.
steps: Product: water, from 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
Combustion forms a new substance and is chemical.
Cooling water vapour into liquid is condensation and is physical.
example.explanation: No carbon dioxide can be assigned to this equation without an additional carbon source.

commonMistakes: Calling condensation the chemical reaction.
Writing H₂ + O₂ → H₂O without balancing.
Predicting carbon dioxide just because a substance burns.

sections.title: Sulfur burning: a gaseous oxide
paragraphs: Sulfur burns in oxygen to form sulfur dioxide. A school equation written using sulfur atoms is S + O₂ → SO₂. Sulfur and oxygen atoms are conserved. The oxygen is incorporated into a gaseous product, so oxygen consumption does not necessarily mean a simple decrease in total gas volume.

Sulfur dioxide is an irritating gas. Describe the expected product rather than using direct inhalation or smell as a test. The phase of the product distinguishes this reaction from magnesium, whose intended oxide product is solid.

Do not infer that every combustion produces carbon dioxide or that all non-metal oxides have identical behaviour. The product formula follows the named reactant and reaction. If a question represents sulfur as S₈ instead, the corresponding balanced equation is S₈ + 8O₂ → 8SO₂.

example.question: Compare the intended oxide products when magnesium and sulfur burn in oxygen. Why is sulfur not a straightforward substitute for iron in a gas-volume oxygen-removal experiment?
steps: Magnesium forms solid MgO; sulfur forms gaseous SO₂.
Sulfur replaces oxygen with another gas unless the product is separately removed.
A gas-volume decrease alone would not directly measure consumed oxygen under that setup.
example.explanation: The distinction uses product identity and phase; it is not a claim that all oxygen-removal methods use metals.

commonMistakes: Calling SO₂ carbon dioxide.
Using smell as a safe identification method.
Assuming that oxygen consumption always removes gas from the gas phase.

sections.title: Carbon dioxide from thermal decomposition
paragraphs: Thermal decomposition uses heat to break a compound into simpler substances. In the school model for copper(II) carbonate, CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. One copper atom, one carbon atom and three oxygen atoms occur on each side. Heating is the condition, not another substance added to the equation.

A typical green copper-carbonate sample becomes black as copper(II) oxide forms. Carbon dioxide makes limewater cloudy because insoluble calcium carbonate forms: CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. It is the precipitate that gives cloudiness; carbon dioxide is not itself a milky gas. Colour change alone does not identify the released gas.

Many metal carbonates give a metal oxide and carbon dioxide on heating, but do not assume every carbonate decomposes under the same conditions. This reaction is not combustion: oxygen is already present in the carbonate, and added oxygen is not required by the equation.

A formula given in a question determines the model you should use. Common laboratory material sold as basic copper(II) carbonate also contains hydroxide and can release water on heating. For CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂, the balanced equation is CuCO₃·Cu(OH)₂ → 2CuO + CO₂ + H₂O. Do not treat every supplied green sample as pure CuCO₃ or silently mix the two formulas.

example.question: For the stated pure-CuCO₃ model, identify the black product and name a test for the released gas. Does the equation require an oxygen reactant?
steps: Black solid: copper(II) oxide, CuO.
Carbon dioxide gives a cloudy limewater result under the usual test conditions.
No O₂ reactant is required: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂.
example.explanation: The answer uses the supplied formula; an actual basic-carbonate sample can also produce water.

commonMistakes: Calling heating a combustion reaction because a flame supplies heat.
Claiming that a colour change proves carbon dioxide formation.
Writing a basic-carbonate equation without its water product.

sections.title: Carbon dioxide and the greenhouse effect
paragraphs: Earth’s surface receives solar energy and emits thermal infrared radiation. Carbon dioxide absorbs some outgoing infrared radiation and the atmosphere emits radiation in different directions, including towards the surface. This changes the rate at which energy is transferred to space; it does not prevent every wavelength or all energy from escaping.

Increasing atmospheric carbon dioxide can strengthen this greenhouse effect. With other influences considered, a changed energy balance can lead to warming and changes in long-term climate patterns. Carbon dioxide does not generate energy from nothing; the explanation concerns transfers of incoming and outgoing energy.

Climate concerns long-term patterns. A single hot day or cold week cannot by itself establish or disprove the effect. The greenhouse effect is also different from ozone depletion: protection from incoming ultraviolet radiation and absorption of outgoing infrared radiation are separate mechanisms. The natural greenhouse effect exists even without a recent increase in carbon dioxide.

example.question: Improve the statement “More carbon dioxide creates heat and stops all radiation escaping.”
steps: Replace creates heat with changes the transfer of outgoing thermal infrared energy.
State that CO₂ absorbs some infrared radiation and atmospheric emission includes downward radiation.
Explain that an increase can alter energy balance and contribute to long-term climate change; some energy still escapes.
example.explanation: The explanation describes a mechanism, not a prediction of the weather on a particular day.

commonMistakes: Explaining warming as an ozone hole.
Saying all heat is permanently trapped.
Using one day’s weather as proof of a long-term climate trend.

sections.title: Water reactions as reactivity evidence
paragraphs: Metals can be compared by their reactions under stated conditions. Potassium, sodium and lithium react with cold water to form their hydroxides and hydrogen; calcium also forms its hydroxide and hydrogen. Within the alkali-metal comparison, potassium is more reactive than sodium, which is more reactive than lithium. Calcium hydroxide is only sparingly soluble, so its mixture may look cloudy.

Magnesium reacts only very slowly with cold water, but heating changes the comparison. With steam the model reaction is Mg + H₂O(g) → MgO + H₂. Cold-water hydroxide and steam oxide products must not be confused. “No visible reaction during this observation” is not identical to “no possible reaction under any conditions”.

Use comparable mass, exposed surface and temperature when interpreting relative vigour. Surface oxide layers and sample shape can affect visible rates. If two metals both show no visible reaction with cold water, that evidence alone cannot rank them against each other. Other reactions are needed; do not invent an order from two negative results.

example.question: Two metals show no visible reaction with cold water during a short observation. Can this alone establish which is more reactive?
steps: Both observations place limits on that particular comparison.
Neither is shown to react faster than the other.
Use additional supplied acid or displacement evidence to rank them.
example.explanation: A negative result is condition-dependent, not a numerical rate or a complete ordering.

commonMistakes: Mixing cold-water and steam observations as if conditions were the same.
Writing magnesium hydroxide as the stated steam product.
Ranking two unreactive-looking samples solely from two negative results.

sections.title: Metals with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid
paragraphs: Many metals above hydrogen in the school reactivity series displace hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid, making a salt and hydrogen gas. Magnesium and zinc provide familiar comparisons; iron also reacts. Copper does not displace hydrogen from these dilute non-oxidizing acids. This is a chemical distinction, not simply a statement that copper reacts a little more slowly.

Balanced examples are Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂; Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂; and Fe + 2HCl → FeCl₂ + H₂. Hydrochloric acid makes chlorides, while sulfuric acid makes sulfates in these examples. The iron product here is iron(II), not automatically iron(III). The acid and conditions must be specified; other acids need not follow this pattern.

A fair rate comparison requires comparable concentration, temperature, sample surface and quantity. Magnesium typically reacts more vigorously than zinc under suitable comparable conditions, while copper gives no hydrogen-displacement result. A protective aluminium oxide layer can delay visible reaction even though aluminium is above zinc and iron in Pearson’s required order. Vigour from unequal samples does not define an intrinsic numerical reactivity scale.

example.question: A question specifies zinc with dilute sulfuric acid. Name the salt and gas, balance the equation and state whether copper would displace hydrogen under the same acid conditions.
steps: Salt: zinc sulfate; gas: hydrogen.
Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂.
Copper does not displace hydrogen from this dilute acid.
example.explanation: The named acid determines the salt, and copper’s position below hydrogen limits this displacement prediction.

commonMistakes: Predicting a chloride from sulfuric acid.
Calling the gas oxygen.
Extending the dilute-acid rule to every acid and concentration.

sections.title: Displacement from aqueous metal salts
paragraphs: In the usual aqueous comparison, a more reactive metal can convert ions of a less reactive metal into the elemental metal. Zinc with copper(II) sulfate gives Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu. The reacting copper species initially is Cu²⁺, not a piece of copper metal or a sulfate ion. Sulfate remains a spectator in the net ionic description.

The net ionic equation is Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. Zinc atoms become ions and copper ions become atoms. Expected evidence includes a copper deposit and a decrease in the blue colour as Cu²⁺ is removed, subject to quantities and completion. Deposit colour depends on surface and particle appearance, so do not require every copper deposit to look identically bright red.

Copper does not displace zinc from zinc sulfate under this usual comparison. A balanced reverse equation is not proof that it happens. Treat the ranking as a prediction for appropriate conditions: very reactive metals in water can react with the solvent, so putting any metal into any aqueous salt is not a universal clean test.

example.question: A hypothetical results table says A displaces B from its salt, and B displaces C. Predict A with C’s salt and C with A’s salt.
steps: The positive evidence gives A > B > C.
A is predicted to displace C under comparable suitable conditions.
C is not predicted to displace A.
example.explanation: This is an original qualitative table, not a performed experiment; solvent reactions or unsuitable conditions can invalidate a simple test.

commonMistakes: Saying sulfate is the displaced element.
Using a balanced reverse equation as evidence of a reaction.
Ignoring the distinction between metal atoms and metal ions.

sections.title: A more reactive metal can remove oxygen from an oxide
paragraphs: A metal above another in the reactivity series can, under suitable reaction conditions, remove oxygen from the less reactive metal’s oxide. The more reactive metal becomes oxidized; the oxide loses oxygen and forms its metal. A model example is Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu.

Here magnesium gains oxygen and copper(II) oxide loses oxygen. Both sides contain one magnesium, one copper and one oxygen atom. The equation predicts product identity and conserves atoms; it does not specify an ignition procedure or guarantee visible reaction on simply mixing cold solids.

Copper is not expected to take oxygen from magnesium oxide in the corresponding simple comparison. State the order, identify which oxide is reduced and give the products. Do not confuse displacement from a solid oxide with metal-ion displacement from a salt solution, even though both can supply evidence of relative reactivity.

example.question: For Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu, which reactant gains oxygen and which loses it? Would Cu + MgO be the expected reverse displacement?
steps: Magnesium gains oxygen to become magnesium oxide.
Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen to form copper.
No expected reverse displacement: copper is below magnesium in the required order.
example.explanation: The oxygen-transfer model connects the ranking to specific reactants and products.

commonMistakes: Claiming copper metal gains oxygen in the forward reaction.
Treating suitable heating conditions as irrelevant to solid reactions.
Writing an unqualified reverse reaction just because atom counts balance.

sections.title: Pearson’s required metal order
paragraphs: Learn the required descending order: potassium > sodium > lithium > calcium > magnesium > aluminium > zinc > iron > copper > silver > gold. Greater-than here means more reactive in this school series; it is not an atomic-number sequence or a claim about every reaction rate.

Use positions to support predictions: zinc is above iron and copper, so it can displace those metals from suitable salts. Aluminium is above zinc despite a surface layer that can hinder observations. Gold is below silver in the stated order. Hydrogen can be added as a comparison reference between iron and copper for the named dilute-acid reactions; it is not one of the eleven metals in this specification list.

Pearson’s chemical reactivity ordering is the required learning target. Do not silently replace it with a list of standard electrode potentials: solvent, passivation and reaction conditions matter, and such tables describe a particular electrochemical comparison. State which evidence supports a ranking when a question supplies results.

example.question: Place aluminium, gold, magnesium, copper and zinc in descending order using the required series.
steps: Magnesium is above aluminium.
Aluminium is above zinc; zinc is above copper.
Copper is above gold: Mg > Al > Zn > Cu > Au.
example.explanation: All five positions follow the source list rather than alphabetical order, density or one uncontrolled demonstration.

commonMistakes: Omitting aluminium because its surface can appear unreactive.
Calling hydrogen one of the listed metals.
Substituting atomic mass or electrode values for the specified order.

sections.title: Rust requires both water and oxygen
paragraphs: Rusting is corrosion of iron in the presence of both water and oxygen. The familiar brown material is commonly described as hydrated iron(III) oxide, with variable water content. Other metals may corrode, but their products are not all called rust.

An oxygen-containing gas with water excluded does not provide both required conditions. Water from which oxygen has been removed and kept excluded likewise lacks one requirement. Ordinary water can contain dissolved oxygen, so “only water in the tube” does not prove oxygen absence.

Salt is not required for rusting but can accelerate corrosion under suitable wet conditions. Rust often flakes and exposes more iron, rather than forming a reliably protective layer. A short observation with no visible brown material does not establish that rusting is impossible; time, surface condition and observation sensitivity also matter.

example.question: A statement says iron rusts only if salt is present. Correct it and name the two required substances.
steps: Both water and oxygen are required.
Salt is not a required reactant in the school conditions test.
Salt water can speed corrosion, so rate and necessity must be distinguished.
example.explanation: A factor that changes a rate need not be essential for the reaction to occur.

commonMistakes: Calling every metal’s corrosion rusting.
Treating clear water as automatically oxygen-free.
Assuming a rust layer permanently seals the iron.

sections.title: Testing rusting conditions without confusing controls
paragraphs: A comparison plan can contrast matched iron samples exposed to water plus air, dry air, and water with oxygen removed and kept excluded. The purpose is to vary availability of one required substance at a time. Keep iron type, surface preparation, exposure time and temperature comparable.

For the dry-air comparison, an appropriate drying arrangement must actually exclude moisture; merely leaving out visible liquid is insufficient because air may contain water vapour. For the oxygen-excluded-water comparison, oxygen removal must be followed by a method that prevents re-entry. Otherwise dissolved or incoming oxygen can invalidate the conclusion.

Record visible changes over sufficient time and explain their limits. Rust in the water-plus-air condition, with no observed rust in the two excluded-condition controls, supports the two-condition explanation. It does not prove exact rate ratios or that controls were perfect. This is a proposed comparison, not results obtained for the site.

example.question: A student calls an open tube of previously oxygen-depleted water an oxygen-free control. Explain the weakness.
steps: Oxygen from the surrounding air can re-enter and dissolve.
Removing oxygen initially is insufficient if it is not kept excluded.
The control may no longer isolate the effect of oxygen absence.
example.explanation: The explanation challenges the control condition, not the requirement for water and oxygen.

commonMistakes: Treating absence of visible bubbles as evidence of no dissolved oxygen.
Changing metal surface and temperature as well as the intended condition.
Presenting a proposed control as a verified trial.

sections.title: Barrier protection: what an intact coating does
paragraphs: Paint, oil, grease or a suitable plastic coating can protect iron by reducing contact with water and oxygen. The mechanism is physical exclusion of the substances needed for rusting. It depends on a sufficiently continuous coating and does not require the coating to donate electrons.

A scratch through an ordinary paint coating exposes iron, so water and oxygen may reach that area. Protection is local: intact regions can remain shielded while exposed iron corrodes. Say what the barrier blocks rather than claiming it changes iron into an unreactive element.

Choose the explanation that fits the material. Oil and grease are useful for some moving surfaces but need maintenance. A zinc coating has an additional sacrificial mechanism discussed below; ordinary paint alone is not the same as galvanising.

example.question: Why can an iron object rust at a deep paint scratch while the intact painted area remains protected?
steps: The scratch exposes iron to water and oxygen.
Intact paint still acts as a barrier elsewhere.
Ordinary paint does not provide the sacrificial electron-transfer protection of a suitable connected reactive metal.
example.explanation: The explanation identifies a local failure of the barrier rather than a mysterious change in iron’s reactivity.

commonMistakes: Claiming paint consumes oxygen until it runs out.
Saying a scratch makes the whole coating vanish.
Calling any coloured coating galvanising.

sections.title: Zinc protection: barrier plus sacrifice
paragraphs: Galvanising coats iron or steel with zinc. An intact zinc layer is a barrier. Zinc is also above iron in the required reactivity series, so connected zinc can oxidize preferentially and protect exposed iron in an appropriate corrosive environment. These are two mechanisms, not two names for ordinary paint.

For zinc oxidation, Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. Sacrificial zinc supplies electrons through the connected metal, reducing iron’s tendency to lose its own electrons. The zinc is consumed and may need replacement. Protection at a scratch is conditional on remaining connected zinc, a suitable environment and the size of exposure; it is not a promise of unlimited protection for every hole.

Sacrificial protection can also use an attached more reactive metal such as magnesium rather than a full coating. Electrical contact matters: an isolated zinc piece nearby is not the same circuit. Copper is below iron, so it is not a suitable sacrificial choice for protecting iron and can worsen corrosion in a connected wet pair.

example.question: Compare deeply scratched ordinary paint with a small scratch in a zinc coating. Why can connected zinc still help, and why is protection not permanent?
steps: Paint’s barrier is broken and gives no sacrificial metal mechanism.
Connected zinc can lose electrons preferentially, helping protect the exposed iron.
Zinc is consumed; contact, environment and remaining material limit protection.
example.explanation: The answer separates exclusion from electron transfer and explains the finite sacrificial resource.

commonMistakes: Calling zinc a less reactive metal than iron.
Saying the iron is sacrificed to protect zinc.
Assuming a disconnected nearby metal always prevents rusting.

sections.title: Oxidation and reduction as oxygen transfer
paragraphs: In the school oxygen-transfer description, oxidation is gain of oxygen and reduction is loss of oxygen. In CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, copper(II) oxide loses oxygen and is reduced; hydrogen gains oxygen and is oxidized. Both changes occur in the same reaction, so it is redox.

The equation conserves one copper atom, one oxygen atom and two hydrogen atoms. Do not classify reduction by a decrease in physical mass alone. The relevant change here is removal of oxygen from the oxide, while the oxygen becomes part of water.

Oxygen transfer is useful for these examples, but not every redox reaction contains oxygen. The electron description extends the idea to metal ions and other species. Conversely, heating, colour change or gas formation alone does not establish redox: carbonate decomposition must not be labelled oxidation simply because heat is used.

example.question: In Mg + CuO → MgO + Cu, name what is oxidized and what is reduced using oxygen transfer.
steps: Magnesium gains oxygen, so it is oxidized.
Copper(II) oxide loses oxygen, so it is reduced.
Both changes occur together: the reaction is redox.
example.explanation: Oxidation and reduction refer to changes in the reactants, not simply to which product is a metal.

commonMistakes: Defining oxidation as any heating.
Calling magnesium reduced because a solid oxide forms.
Saying oxygen must appear as O₂ in every redox reaction.

sections.title: Oxidation loses electrons; reduction gains them
paragraphs: Oxidation is electron loss and reduction is electron gain. For zinc with copper(II) ions, zinc oxidation is Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and copper-ion reduction is Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Each half-equation conserves atoms and total charge.

Adding the two halves cancels two electrons and gives Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu. The electrons leave zinc and are accepted by copper ions; they are not left as extra products in the overall equation. Sulfate ions cancel as spectators if the starting solution is copper(II) sulfate.

A gain of negative electrons makes the ion’s charge less positive in this example: Cu²⁺ becomes neutral Cu. It is the reactant Cu²⁺ that gains electrons and is reduced. A charge change should be explained by the direction and number of electrons, not by treating a superscript as a count of copper atoms.

example.question: Classify Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. Check each charge balance.
steps: Iron(II) loses one electron, so it is oxidized; right charge +3−1 = +2.
Copper(II) gains two electrons, so it is reduced; left charge +2−2 = 0.
One atom of the named element is present on each side of each half-equation.
example.explanation: The classifications depend on electron transfer, not oxygen presence. These two halves are separate classification tasks and are not presented as a combined spontaneous reaction.

commonMistakes: Writing electrons on the wrong side of a half-equation.
Calling electron gain oxidation.
Cancelling unequal numbers of electrons without multiplying a half-equation.

sections.title: Identify an agent by what it does to the other reactant
paragraphs: An oxidizing agent causes another reactant to lose electrons; it accepts those electrons and is itself reduced. A reducing agent donates electrons and causes another reactant to gain them; the donor is itself oxidized. The agent’s name describes its effect on the other substance, not its own change.

In Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, zinc is the reducing agent and is oxidized. Copper(II) ions are the oxidizing agent and are reduced. Name the actual species Cu²⁺, not the copper product, and do not assign the role to unchanged sulfate ions.

In the oxygen-transfer example CuO + H₂ → Cu + H₂O, CuO supplies oxygen to hydrogen and is the oxidizing agent; H₂ removes oxygen from CuO and is the reducing agent. Oxygen gain/loss and electron bookkeeping agree for these examples. A reaction can have an oxidizing agent even when no free oxygen gas is a reactant.

example.question: For Zn + Cu²⁺ → Zn²⁺ + Cu, complete the four roles: oxidized reactant, reduced reactant, reducing agent, oxidizing agent.
steps: Oxidized reactant: Zn; reduced reactant: Cu²⁺.
Reducing agent: Zn, which donates electrons.
Oxidizing agent: Cu²⁺, which accepts electrons.
example.explanation: The donor’s own oxidation and the acceptor’s own reduction are the reason the two agent names can initially seem reversed.

commonMistakes: Calling the oxidized reactant the oxidizing agent just because the words look similar.
Naming product Cu instead of reacting Cu²⁺ as the oxidizing agent.
Calling sulfate the agent merely because it occurs in the salt formula.

sections.title: Planning the named acid–metal investigation
paragraphs: The named school investigation compares magnesium, zinc and iron with dilute hydrochloric and sulfuric acids. Keep each metal/acid combination identifiable in a results table, recording reaction evidence and whether a gas is detected. Interpret a proposed table separately from measured results: no investigation has been performed for this site.

When changing the metal, keep the acid identity, concentration, volume and initial temperature comparable, and account for metal quantity, exposed surface and surface condition. Use a consistent start and observation interval. When investigating acid identity instead, hold the chosen metal and other stated conditions constant. Equal molar concentrations of different acids do not automatically mean equal available hydrogen-ion concentration, so avoid treating acid identity as an irrelevant variable.

Gas evidence supports hydrogen formation, with an appropriate school hydrogen identification test providing more information than fizzing alone. Slower evolution may not give a suitable gas sample in a short observation, so a weak test result is not automatically proof of a different gas. Dilute acids and flammable hydrogen require the school’s controlled practical arrangements; the examples do not propose adding alkali metals to acid.

The expected salt follows the acid: magnesium chloride, zinc chloride and iron(II) chloride with HCl; corresponding sulfates with dilute H₂SO₄. Example balanced equations are Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ and Fe + H₂SO₄ → FeSO₄ + H₂. Link a recorded observation to a justified product, then explain what the comparison can and cannot establish.

example.question: A planned zinc/iron comparison uses different hydrochloric-acid concentrations and different surface areas. Identify two changes needed for a fairer comparison and name the expected gas.
steps: Use the same stated acid concentration for both metal comparisons.
Make exposed surfaces comparable, while controlling the other stated conditions.
Expected gas: hydrogen; fizzing alone is not a conclusive identification.
example.explanation: This is an original plan review, not a trial result. Changing several conditions at once weakens a reactivity inference.

commonMistakes: Recording invented observations as if the practical was performed.
Calling every acid comparison fair merely because the solution volumes match.
Writing iron(III) sulfate as the automatic product of iron with the named dilute acid.

sections.title: Rates, endpoints and limits of acid–metal evidence
paragraphs: A quantitative comparison may record hydrogen volume against time using a suitable school collection setup. An average gas-production rate over a stated interval is change in gas volume divided by elapsed time, with units such as cm³ s⁻¹. Compare like intervals and methods, check collection losses and repeat measurements rather than ranking from an isolated bubble count.

Total gas at completion and rate are different quantities. Final hydrogen amount depends on available reactants and the limiting reactant. Equal masses of different metals do not give equal numbers of metal atoms, so a larger final volume is not by itself evidence of greater reactivity. A faster initial change and a larger final amount answer different questions.

A slow start can reflect a surface oxide layer, as in aluminium with hydrochloric acid, rather than a low position in the required series. A reaction can also slow because a poorly soluble product coats the surface, as calcium sulfate can do in the appropriate calcium/sulfuric-acid comparison. Neither extension is a recommendation to replace the named school samples or perform a new trial.

A stopped reaction does not always prove that both reactants are exhausted. Surface coating, limiting-reactant exhaustion or changing conditions can give different explanations; use the supplied evidence to distinguish them. Report uncertainty and the scope of the comparison, without claiming that repeated similar values eliminate every systematic error.

example.question: Two hypothetical trials each collect 20 cm³ of gas: A takes 10 s and B takes 40 s. Calculate the average rates to that volume. Does equal final gas volume prove equal rates?
steps: A’s average to this volume is four times B’s; equal amount does not mean equal rate.
example.explanation: Invented arithmetic illustrates amount versus rate. It does not establish an intrinsic metal ranking without matched reaction and collection conditions.

commonMistakes: Ranking reactivity solely by total hydrogen volume from equal metal masses.
Using volume multiplied by time as a rate.
Assuming that a stalled coated surface means all acid has reacted.

sections.title: Ores, compounds and native metals — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Most metals are obtained from ores in the Earth’s crust. An ore contains a useful metal or its compounds in a concentration that makes extraction worthwhile under the stated circumstances. It is usually a mixture of minerals and other material, rather than a pure metal compound with one formula.

Reactive metals tend to occur combined with other elements. Obtaining metal from a compound requires a chemical change: iron atoms in an oxide are not simply loose iron pieces that a magnet can pull out. Crushing or separating unwanted rock can concentrate the useful material, but it does not by itself reduce metal ions to the metal.

Less reactive metals can occur as the uncombined element, often called native metal. Gold is a familiar example. “Often found uncombined” is a tendency, not a claim that every sample of an unreactive metal is pure or that such metals never occur in compounds. Extraction method depends on the actual starting material as well as the metal.

example.question: A supplied ore contains iron oxide mixed with unwanted rock. Explain why separating the rock is not the same as obtaining iron metal.
steps: Separation can increase the proportion of iron oxide.
Iron remains chemically combined with oxygen in the oxide.
A chemical reduction is needed to form elemental iron.
example.explanation: This distinguishes concentration of a mixture from changing the chemical species.

commonMistakes: Calling every ore a pure compound.
Treating an oxide as a mixture of free metal and oxygen.
Claiming every unreactive metal occurs only in native form.

sections.title: Carbon-based extraction of iron — Paper 2C
paragraphs: For the school extraction comparison, place carbon below aluminium and above zinc and iron in the reactivity series. Metals below carbon can often be extracted from suitable oxides by carbon-based reduction. Iron illustrates this method; aluminium is too reactive for the corresponding simple carbon reduction of its oxide.

In the familiar iron process, carbon helps produce carbon monoxide, which reduces iron oxide. An illustrative balanced equation is Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂. Iron oxide loses oxygen and is reduced; carbon monoxide gains oxygen and is oxidized. There are two iron, three carbon and six oxygen atoms on each side.

The reactivity rule supports method selection, rather than a complete factory design. Actual choices also depend on the compound, unwanted products, available energy and process information. A metal below carbon is not necessarily extracted by exactly the same sequence as iron, and carbon is not itself a metal.

example.question: Explain the different school extraction choices for iron and aluminium using their positions relative to carbon.
steps: Iron is below carbon, allowing the illustrated carbon-based reduction route.
Aluminium is above carbon, so this simple route does not remove it from its oxide.
Aluminium is instead obtained by electrolysis of an appropriate molten electrolyte.
example.explanation: The answer uses relative reactivity; it does not require memorizing a complete furnace sequence.

commonMistakes: Using copper rather than carbon as the extraction-method boundary.
Calling CO the iron product.
Saying a balanced equation alone guarantees a suitable industrial route.

sections.title: Why aluminium extraction uses electrolysis — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Aluminium oxide is strongly bound in the school reactivity comparison, so aluminium extraction uses electrolysis. In the industrial example, alumina is dissolved in a molten cryolite-based bath. The electrolyte has mobile ions; electrical energy drives the extraction. Solid ionic material with fixed ions would not serve the same conducting role.

Aluminium ions gain electrons at the negative cathode: Al³⁺ + 3e⁻ → Al. Charge is conserved because +3 − 3 = 0. The example uses a molten electrolyte, not ordinary aqueous aluminium-salt electrolysis, where competing reactions can prevent the intended metal deposit.

A carbon anode in the conventional process is consumed as oxygen-containing species react with it, producing carbon oxides. Carbon’s presence as an electrode does not mean it directly reduces aluminium oxide by the simple below-carbon extraction rule. Heating and a large electrical supply are inputs that should be considered when evaluating a supplied process.

example.question: A student says a carbon electrode proves aluminium is extracted by heating its oxide with carbon. Correct the explanation.
steps: The aluminium extraction example is electrolysis of an appropriate molten electrolyte.
Al³⁺ gains three electrons at the cathode.
Carbon can act as a consumed anode without making the process simple carbon reduction of aluminium oxide.
example.explanation: An electrode material and the extraction method are separate parts of the explanation.

commonMistakes: Trying to apply the molten result automatically to aqueous aluminium salts.
Writing Al³⁺ → Al + 3e⁻ for cathode reduction.
Confusing alumina with elemental aluminium.

sections.title: Evaluate a process from the supplied information — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Use the information given about starting material, reduction or electrolysis, recovery, energy and waste. A reasoned comment connects a piece of evidence to an advantage or limitation. Pearson explicitly says detailed knowledge of every specific extraction process is not required for this point; an unfamiliar diagram can still be interpreted using chemistry and supplied data.

Original model: 100 kg of ore contains 20% Fe₂O₃ by mass, with the rest specified as material containing no iron. Given relative atomic masses Fe = 56 and O = 16, Fe₂O₃ has relative formula mass 160 and an iron fraction 112/160. The 20 kg oxide can therefore yield at most 14 kg iron. If recovery is 80% of that theoretical iron, actual recovered iron is 11.2 kg. Ore grade, theoretical yield and recovery are different quantities.

Compare alternatives on the same basis, such as energy per kilogram of recovered metal rather than energy per batch of unequal size. Higher recovery may reduce unused metal-containing waste, while higher energy demand may bring a different cost or environmental trade-off. Use the stated electricity source and waste treatment information; a high current alone does not establish a specific carbon footprint.

Give a qualified conclusion and name missing evidence. No single favourable number proves that a process is best overall. These example values are invented and are not an operating plant’s measurements or current market prices.

example.question: Two invented processes recover 10 kg metal using 50 MJ and 15 kg using 90 MJ. Which uses less energy per kilogram? What would you need before recommending one overall?
steps: First:50/10 = 5 MJ kg⁻¹.
Second:90/15 = 6 MJ kg⁻¹; the first has lower energy per recovered kilogram.
Overall judgement also needs comparable product quality, waste, other inputs and relevant impacts.
example.explanation: Normalizing to the recovered product permits a fairer energy comparison without inventing a complete industrial assessment.

commonMistakes: Treating 20% oxide in an ore as 20% elemental iron.
Applying recovery to the wrong starting mass.
Comparing unequal batches solely by total energy.

sections.title: Choose aluminium or copper by the useful property — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Aluminium has low density, so aluminium alloys are useful where low mass matters, such as aircraft components. Pure aluminium is relatively soft; alloying can supply the required mechanical strength. A thin protective oxide layer contributes to corrosion resistance even though aluminium is high in the reactivity series.

Aluminium conducts heat, helping cooking utensils transfer energy to their contents, and is malleable enough for forming and foil. State the property relevant to the particular use: low density does not explain heat transfer, and good thermal conductivity does not by itself establish aircraft strength.

Copper’s electrical conductivity and ductility make it suitable for electrical wiring: it carries current and can be drawn into wires. Its thermal conductivity is useful in heat exchangers, while its workability and resistance to corrosion under suitable conditions support some plumbing uses. Copper still can corrode; relatively unreactive is not the same as indestructible.

example.question: For copper wire, explain why both electrical conductivity and ductility are useful. For an aircraft component, explain why specifying an aluminium alloy is more informative than simply saying pure aluminium.
steps: Conductivity permits current flow; ductility permits drawing into wire.
Low density helps reduce aircraft mass.
An appropriate alloy can provide greater strength than pure aluminium.
example.explanation: A material choice needs the relevant combination of properties, rather than a list unrelated to the use.

commonMistakes: Using low density as the explanation for copper electrical conduction.
Calling pure aluminium automatically strong enough for every structural use.
Treating corrosion resistance as a guarantee of no reaction in any environment.

sections.title: Iron and the three required steel types — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Iron’s magnetic behaviour is useful in magnetic components; appropriate soft iron can be magnetized readily for an electromagnet core. Iron is also the main metal in steel, whose composition and treatment give a range of mechanical properties. Explain the selected material, rather than treating pure iron and every steel as interchangeable.

Low-carbon or mild steel is relatively easy to shape and weld, making it useful for formed vehicle panels and many structural products. High-carbon steel can be harder and better able to retain a cutting edge, supporting cutting-tool uses, but often sacrifices ease of shaping and toughness compared with a suitable lower-carbon steel.

Stainless steel contains chromium, which supports a protective surface layer and corrosion resistance. This is useful for cutlery and equipment exposed to moisture. Many grades also contain other elements, but nickel is not compulsory in every stainless steel. “Stainless” means corrosion-resistant under appropriate conditions, not immune to every chemical environment.

The required comparison is low-carbon, high-carbon and stainless steel. Heat treatment and grade affect real properties, so avoid a universal claim that increasing carbon always improves every property or that every stainless steel is non-magnetic. Match hardness, formability or corrosion resistance to the task being described.

example.question: Choose a required steel type for an easily formed panel, a cutting edge and corrosion-resistant cutlery, explaining one property for each.
steps: Mild steel:relatively easy to form for the panel.
Appropriate high-carbon steel:hardness and edge retention for the tool.
Stainless steel:chromium-supported corrosion resistance for the cutlery.
example.explanation: The choices illustrate school property–use links, not an engineering specification for every real product.

commonMistakes: Calling hardness and toughness the same property.
Claiming all stainless steels must contain nickel or be non-magnetic.
Using more carbon as a promise of improvement in every property.

sections.title: An alloy is a mixture — Paper 2C
paragraphs: An alloy is a mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements, usually other metals or carbon. Steel contains iron with carbon and may contain additional elements. Carbon is a non-metal, so an alloy does not have to consist only of metals.

Composition can vary between grades, changing properties. An alloy is not normally represented by a single fixed formula like an ionic compound. A stated percentage describes one selected composition, not a universal ratio for every sample carrying that alloy name.

Alloys retain useful metallic behaviour while allowing properties to be adjusted. Changing composition can improve one property while reducing another, so specify the desired feature. The simple mixture description is the requirement here; it does not imply that every atom is arranged randomly or that all metallurgical phases are identical.

example.question: An invented steel specification gives 0.5% carbon by mass. How much carbon is in 2.0 kg of that material? Does this mean every steel has the same composition?
steps: Carbon mass = .005 × 2.0 kg = .010 kg = 10 g.
No:the percentage defines this supplied composition.
Other steels can have different carbon content and additional elements.
example.explanation: This is an original composition calculation; carbon does not need to be a metal for the mixture to qualify as an alloy.

commonMistakes: Defining an alloy as exactly two metals.
Calling the given percentage a fixed chemical formula.
Calculating 0.5 × 2.0 instead of converting percent to a fraction.

sections.title: Different atom sizes can hinder sliding — Paper 2C
paragraphs: In a simple pure-metal model, similarly sized atoms form regular arrangements that can slide as the material deforms. Different-sized alloying atoms disrupt that regularity. The distorted arrangement makes the movements responsible for plastic deformation harder, so a greater force is needed and the material can be harder than the pure metal.

Use the full reasoning chain: different atom sizes → distortion of the regular arrangement → harder movement → increased resistance to deformation. Saying only “there are two elements” does not explain why sliding changes. Do not say that the alloy has more layers or that all metallic bonds disappear.
