The diagram is an original two-dimensional schematic, not a microscopic photograph or a measured atomic structure. It shows a substituted larger atom as one way to illustrate distortion. Actual alloys can also contain small atoms between metal atoms and several phases; their properties depend on composition and treatment. The school model does not imply that deformation becomes impossible or that every alloy is harder under every comparison.

example.question: Improve the answer “An alloy is harder because it contains another element.”
steps: Explain that atoms of a different size disturb the regular metal arrangement.
Link the distortion to more difficult sliding or plastic deformation.
State that more force is required to deform the material, giving greater hardness in this model.
example.explanation: The explanation connects composition to structure and then to a mechanical property.

commonMistakes: Saying atoms cannot move at all in an alloy.
Explaining hardness as the presence of more electrons without a sliding mechanism.
Treating the schematic as an actual measured arrangement.

diagram.alt: Original two-dimensional model: uniform atoms in regular rows beside an alloy region with a larger substituted atom and nearby displaced atoms; distortion hinders plastic movement.
diagram.caption: Original schematic of one alloy-hardening mechanism. Sizes and positions are illustrative, not measured; real structures and treatment can vary.

sections.title: Use the correct indicator colour
paragraphs: In the usual school comparisons, litmus is red in sufficiently acidic solution and blue in alkaline solution. Blue litmus changing red is evidence of acidity; red litmus changing blue is evidence of alkalinity. A strip that keeps its starting colour does not on its own establish neutrality.

Phenolphthalein is colourless in acidic and neutral solution, and pink in suitably alkaline solution. Methyl orange is red in sufficiently acidic solution and yellow on the alkaline side of its transition; at pH 7 it is yellow, not orange. Orange is an intermediate transition colour for methyl orange, rather than a universal signal for neutral solution.

Indicators change over a range of pH, rather than at a single value for every indicator. Some weakly acidic solutions already give methyl orange its yellow colour; some slightly alkaline solutions still leave phenolphthalein colourless. Use the named indicator and the context, and use a broader-range test when an exact acid/alkali classification is uncertain.

example.question: An invented sample leaves phenolphthalein colourless. A student concludes that its pH is exactly 7. Explain why this is not established.
steps: Acidic solution can also leave phenolphthalein colourless.
The indicator has a transition range and does not measure an exact pH.
A suitable pH measurement or universal-indicator comparison would give more information.
example.explanation: One indicator colour can correspond to many pH values.

commonMistakes: Calling methyl orange orange at every neutral point.
Calling colourless phenolphthalein proof of a neutral solution.
Confusing the colour of a reagent with a measured pH.

sections.title: Classify a solution on the pH scale
paragraphs: For Pearson’s 0–14 school scale, classify pH 0–3 as strongly acidic, 4–6 as weakly acidic, 7 as neutral, 8–10 as weakly alkaline and 11–14 as strongly alkaline. Lower pH means a more acidic aqueous solution; higher pH means a more alkaline one under the stated conditions.

The words strongly acidic and weakly acidic here classify the solution’s pH. They are not the same as defining a strong or weak acid by how completely it ionizes. Concentration also matters: a very dilute strong acid need not have the same pH as a concentrated sample of that acid.

Use the measurement provided, rather than assuming a solution is neutral because it looks colourless or contains a salt. The familiar neutral pH of 7 is the school reference near room temperature; the classification task does not require deriving a logarithmic formula.

example.question: Classify invented solutions with pH 2, 5, 7, 9 and 12 using the required scale.
steps: 2: strongly acidic; 5: weakly acidic.
7: neutral.
9: weakly alkaline; 12: strongly alkaline.
example.explanation: These labels describe the supplied solutions, without identifying the acid or its concentration.

commonMistakes: Using pH 7 as acidic.
Equating the pH label with complete versus partial acid ionization.
Assuming every salt solution has pH 7.

sections.title: Estimate pH with universal indicator
paragraphs: Universal indicator combines indicator responses to cover a broad pH range. Compare the sample’s resulting colour with the chart for that formulation: commonly red/orange/yellow towards the acidic end, green near neutral, and blue/purple towards the alkaline end. The supplied chart, rather than an invented exact hue, determines the estimate.

Use a clean separate sample or indicator paper according to the specified method, avoiding contamination between solutions. Compare against a light background and follow the chart’s instructions. Strongly coloured or cloudy samples, ambiguous lighting and a colour between chart bands can limit the estimate.

Report an approximate pH or a justified interval. Universal indicator is not a precise electronic pH measurement and is generally less suitable than a chosen single indicator for a sharp titration end point. A colour sequence across the whole scale does not mean every colour change happens at neutralization.

example.question: A supplied chart places the observed colour between pH 5 and 6. What conclusion is justified?
steps: Estimate pH between about 5 and 6.
Classify it as weakly acidic on Pearson’s school scale.
Do not report an unsupported value such as 5.37.
example.explanation: The precision of the conclusion follows the resolution of the evidence.

commonMistakes: Reporting several decimal places from a broad colour band.
Ignoring the chart supplied with the indicator.
Using universal indicator as an exact neutralization meter.

sections.title: Acids supply H⁺; alkalis supply OH⁻
paragraphs: In the aqueous school description, acids provide hydrogen ions, H⁺, and alkalis provide hydroxide ions, OH⁻. For example, hydrochloric acid supplies H⁺ and Cl⁻, while sodium hydroxide solution contains Na⁺ and OH⁻. The ions move in solution; their charges and names matter.

H⁺ is shorthand for a hydrogen ion associated with water in an aqueous solution, rather than a free isolated proton travelling through otherwise empty space. This notation is sufficient for the required neutralization equation. The chloride and sodium ions do not disappear merely because H⁺ and OH⁻ react.

An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to give an alkaline solution. An insoluble metal oxide can be a base without being an alkali. Ammonia can also accept a proton and produce OH⁻ through its reaction with water, even though NH₃ itself has no OH group in its formula.

example.question: Identify the ions responsible for acidity and alkalinity in the school equations for hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution.
steps: Acidity: H⁺ from the aqueous acid.
Alkalinity: OH⁻ from the alkali.
Cl⁻ and Na⁺ are other ions, not the reacting acid/alkali pair in the net equation.
example.explanation: The answer distinguishes reacting ions from spectator ions.

commonMistakes: Writing H⁻ for a hydrogen ion from an acid.
Confusing hydroxide OH⁻ with an oxygen atom.
Defining every base as a soluble hydroxide.

sections.title: Neutralization uses reacting amounts, not equal volumes
paragraphs: An alkali can neutralize an acid. For a metal-hydroxide alkali, the net ionic equation is H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l). One proton and one hydroxide ion combine to give water; total charge is zero on both sides. The other ions can remain in the resulting salt solution.

For hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide, HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. For sulfuric acid and sodium hydroxide, full neutralization is H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O. The second equation requires two hydroxide amounts per sulfuric-acid amount in this school comparison.

Equal volumes only give the appropriate reacting ratio when the concentrations and equation support it. Adding too much alkali leaves an alkaline excess; too little can leave acid. The stoichiometric point and an indicator’s visible end point are related but distinct, and the pH after neutralization is not 7 for every possible acid/base pair.

example.question: Given equal concentrations and complete neutralization as written, compare the NaOH volumes needed for equal volumes of HCl and H₂SO₄.
steps: HCl:NaOH reacting ratio is 1:1.
H₂SO₄:NaOH reacting ratio is 1:2.
The sulfuric-acid sample needs twice the NaOH volume under these stated conditions.
example.explanation: The conclusion depends on both the balanced equation and the stated concentrations.

commonMistakes: Assuming all neutralizations need equal volumes.
Removing spectator ions from existence.
Calling every indicator end point exactly pH 7.

sections.title: Set up an acid–alkali titration — Paper 2C
paragraphs: A titration measures the volume needed to react with a measured portion of another solution. In the illustrative school setup, use a volumetric pipette with a filler for a fixed alkali portion in a conical flask and a clamped burette for acid. Clean the apparatus; final rinses of the burette and pipette use the solutions they will contain, avoiding dilution by remaining water.

Rinse the conical flask with distilled water, add the measured alkali and a few drops of a suitable indicator, and place it over a white tile. Fill the burette and its tip, remove the filling funnel and record the initial reading. A starting value of exactly zero is unnecessary: the delivered volume is found from the difference in readings.

Carry out a rough run to locate the end point. In accurate runs, swirl to mix, wash splashes on the flask walls down with distilled water, and add titrant dropwise near the end point. Stop at the specified lasting colour change. For acid added to NaOH with phenolphthalein, the pink colour just disappears; adding alkali to acid gives the opposite direction.

Use eye-level readings and the appropriate meniscus for the solution, normally the bottom for a clear aqueous liquid. Use the pipette as calibrated rather than blowing out a remaining drop indiscriminately. These are descriptions for a supervised laboratory method, not a claim that an experiment has been carried out here.

example.question: Explain why the conical flask can contain a little distilled water, but a pipette containing residual water must be conditioned with its measured solution.
steps: Water in the flask does not change the transferred reacting amount.
Residual water in the pipette can dilute the measured solution.
The two vessels have different measurement roles.
example.explanation: Concentration and reacting amount are separate; water affects them differently in these steps.

commonMistakes: Rinsing the flask with extra alkali, adding an unmeasured reacting amount.
Leaving an air bubble in the delivery tip.
Requiring an initial burette reading of zero.

sections.title: Calculate a titre and evaluate repeat results — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Titre = final burette reading − initial burette reading. The scale normally increases down the burette, so the difference is positive for solution delivered. Record the units and the precision supported by the actual apparatus. Two readings are involved, so a delivery result depends on both readings.

Repeat accurate titrations to obtain concordant results using the tolerance specified by the task or laboratory method. Do not silently choose a universal tolerance: different teaching methods can specify different acceptable differences. Exclude a rough locating run from the reported accurate mean and explain any discarded anomalous result.

Original example: 2.15 to 26.35 cm³ gives 24.20 cm³; 1.05 to 25.35 cm³ gives 24.30 cm³. For a supplied tolerance of at most 0.10 cm³, these agree sufficiently, and their mean is 24.25 cm³. A rough result of 26.50 cm³ is not included.

Close repeats demonstrate repeatability, not guaranteed accuracy. All runs could share an end-point bias, contaminated solution or an incorrectly calibrated instrument. Overshooting the end point increases the delivered titre; interpreting the effect on a calculated concentration then requires the actual equation and calculation setup.

example.question: Use the two original accurate titres 24.20 and 24.30 cm³ and a stated tolerance of at most 0.10 cm³. Calculate their difference and mean.
steps: Difference = 0.10 cm³, within the stated inclusive tolerance.
The rough run is excluded; repeatability is not a proof of absence of bias.
example.explanation: The example applies a supplied rule, rather than promoting a local tolerance into a Pearson-wide requirement.

commonMistakes: Averaging a rough run with accurate runs.
Subtracting final from initial.
Claiming close repeats prove the true value.

sections.title: Recognize the broadly soluble ionic families
paragraphs: The required general rules treat common sodium, potassium and ammonium compounds as soluble in water, and all nitrates as soluble. These rules help choose aqueous starting reagents: lead(II) nitrate can provide dissolved Pb²⁺, despite many other lead salts being poorly soluble.

Common chlorides and sulfates are usually soluble, subject to the named exceptions in the following section. Common carbonates and hydroxides are usually insoluble, subject to their own exceptions. Identify both ions before choosing a rule: a compound is not classified solely from whether it contains a metal.

Solubility describes whether appreciable material can dissolve under the stated conditions; it is not the same as whether a material reacts with water. A sparingly soluble substance has a finite solubility. These school rules make predictions for common compounds, not numerical solubility values at every temperature or concentration.

example.question: Predict whether sodium carbonate, ammonium nitrate and lead(II) nitrate can be used as soluble starting compounds under the school rules.
steps: Sodium carbonate: soluble because it is a common sodium compound.
Ammonium nitrate: soluble by both relevant broad rules.
Lead(II) nitrate: soluble because it is a nitrate.
example.explanation: Use the complete ion pair and the named rule, rather than extending the behaviour of one lead compound to all of them.

commonMistakes: Calling all compounds of lead insoluble.
Assuming all carbonates are insoluble.
Confusing dissolving with chemical decomposition.

sections.title: Learn the required solubility exceptions
paragraphs: Common chlorides are soluble except silver chloride and lead(II) chloride. Common sulfates are soluble except those of barium, calcium and lead(II), which Pearson places in the insoluble group for these predictions. Do not omit calcium sulfate because another simplified chart uses a different cutoff.

Common carbonates are insoluble except sodium, potassium and ammonium carbonates. Common hydroxides are insoluble except those of sodium, potassium and calcium; calcium hydroxide is only slightly soluble. Its dissolved portion still produces an alkaline solution, such as clear limewater.

Use these exact required families to predict a precipitate when appropriate aqueous ions are mixed. “Insoluble” is a school classification, not zero dissolved ions under every condition. Very dilute mixtures may not give a visible precipitate, and the appearance alone is not proof that an isolated solid is pure.

example.question: Classify AgCl, MgSO₄, CaSO₄, Na₂CO₃ and Ca(OH)₂ using the required rules.
steps: AgCl: insoluble; MgSO₄: soluble.
CaSO₄: in the required insoluble sulfate exceptions; Na₂CO₃: soluble.
Ca(OH)₂: slightly soluble, with its dissolved portion alkaline.
example.explanation: The answer preserves Pearson’s named exceptions and the calcium-hydroxide qualification.

commonMistakes: Treating calcium hydroxide as freely soluble like sodium hydroxide.
Forgetting the sulfate exceptions.
Claiming an insoluble salt has absolutely no dissolved ions.

sections.title: Follow the proton from donor to acceptor
paragraphs: In the proton-transfer description, an acid donates H⁺ and a base accepts H⁺. Follow the transferred proton and identify the reacting species: the acid has lost a proton and the base has gained one. A proton is not an electron, so this description must not be confused with the electron transfer used to define redox.

For H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, hydroxide accepts the proton. For NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺, ammonia accepts a proton to form ammonium. The latter balances three starting hydrogen atoms plus one transferred proton to give four, and charge zero plus one to give +1.

With water, NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻: ammonia accepts a proton from water. Here water acts as a proton donor; in another reaction it can be a proton acceptor. Assign roles from the particular reaction, rather than insisting every substance has the same role in every situation.

example.question: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, name the proton donor and acceptor in the forward direction.
steps: H₂O donates a proton, leaving OH⁻.
NH₃ accepts it, forming NH₄⁺.
Water is the acid and ammonia the base for this direction.
example.explanation: The atom and charge changes reveal the roles directly.

commonMistakes: Saying ammonia donates the proton because it contains hydrogen.
Replacing proton transfer with electron transfer.
Calling NH₄⁺ neutral.

sections.title: Bases include oxides, hydroxides and ammonia
paragraphs: Metal oxides, metal hydroxides and ammonia can act as bases in the required examples. A base neutralizes an acid by accepting protons; it need not contain an OH group in its written formula. Copper(II) oxide is a familiar insoluble basic oxide used for salt preparation.

An alkali is a base soluble in water that gives an alkaline solution. Sodium hydroxide is an alkali; copper(II) oxide is a base but is not an alkali. Slightly soluble calcium hydroxide gives OH⁻ in the dissolved portion. Aqueous ammonia accepts protons from water and is alkaline, without being a bottle of molecular NH₄OH.

Avoid extending the example to every oxide: some oxides are acidic or have other acid–base behaviour. In a particular school question, identify the named reactant and use the appropriate reaction. The base/alkali distinction is about solubility and aqueous behaviour, not a ranking of which material is safest or most reactive.

example.question: Explain why CuO can prepare a salt from an acid even though it is not an alkali.
steps: CuO acts as a base and reacts with acid.
It does not dissolve appreciably in water to form an alkali.
Base is the broader category; alkali is a soluble-base category.
example.explanation: The two descriptions are compatible, rather than contradictory.

commonMistakes: Calling all bases alkalis.
Requiring every base formula to contain OH.
Calling every metal oxide strongly alkaline in water.

sections.title: Acid–metal reactions form the named salt
paragraphs: Suitable reactive metals with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid can form a salt and hydrogen. Hydrochloric acid gives chlorides; sulfuric acid gives sulfates. For example, Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂ and Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂. Match the salt formula to the metal ion’s charge.

Bubbles suggest a gas but do not identify it alone. The standard supervised hydrogen test gives a squeaky pop with a lighted splint. A metal below hydrogen, such as copper, does not give the same hydrogen-producing reaction with these dilute non-oxidizing acids under the usual conditions.

Pearson explicitly excludes nitric-acid reactions with metals from this requirement. Do not apply the salt + hydrogen pattern to them. Reaction rate, surface coating and insoluble salt layers can also affect observations; the separately taught 2.21 practical examines the named Mg/Zn/Fe dilute-acid comparisons.

example.question: Give the salt and gas in the illustrated reaction of magnesium with dilute sulfuric acid, and state whether the same rule should be applied to copper or to nitric-acid metal reactions.
steps: Salt: magnesium sulfate; gas: hydrogen.
Copper does not follow this hydrogen-producing pattern with the named dilute acids.
Nitric-acid metal reactions are excluded from this point.
example.explanation: The general pattern has stated reactants and boundaries.

commonMistakes: Naming a chloride when the acid is sulfuric.
Extending hydrogen formation to every metal and acid.
Using bubbles alone as complete gas identification.

sections.title: Acids react with basic oxides, hydroxides and ammonia
paragraphs: A suitable metal oxide or metal hydroxide with acid produces a salt and water. Examples are CuO + 2HCl → CuCl₂ + H₂O, CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O and CuO + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O. The acid supplies chloride, sulfate or nitrate; Cu²⁺ determines how many anions are needed.

For hydroxides, match the amount of H⁺ to the OH groups: Mg(OH)₂ + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + 2H₂O. Brackets in Mg(OH)₂ represent two complete hydroxide groups, rather than changing the formula of water to balance an equation.

Ammonia with acid can form an ammonium salt without water as an additional product in the overall equation: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl. This is proton acceptance by ammonia. Do not add water automatically to every acid–base equation or treat ammonia as a metal.

example.question: Write a balanced equation for copper(II) oxide with nitric acid. Explain why two nitrates occur in the salt.
steps: CuO + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.
Cu²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻ ions for electrical neutrality.
The equation balances Cu1, N2, H2 and O7 on each side.
example.explanation: Charge determines the salt formula; coefficients then conserve atoms.

commonMistakes: Writing CuNO₃ for copper(II) nitrate.
Changing compound subscripts to balance.
Adding water as a compulsory product of ammonia with HCl.

sections.title: Carbonates give a salt, water and carbon dioxide
paragraphs: A suitable metal carbonate with acid forms a salt, water and carbon dioxide. An original illustration is CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂. Replacing the acid with nitric acid gives Ca(NO₃)₂ as the salt, while sulfuric acid gives a sulfate subject to solubility and reaction-layer effects.

Effervescence is an observation of gas release. Carbon dioxide can be identified by its clouding of limewater in the usual test, rather than by the absence of a hydrogen pop. Calcium carbonate with sulfuric acid can become coated by poorly soluble calcium sulfate, slowing reaction; a stopped reaction does not automatically mean all the starting carbonate was used.

Choose the acid to supply the desired salt anion and check whether that salt is soluble. For a soluble-salt preparation from an insoluble carbonate, a suitable excess of the solid can consume the acid before filtration, but the product’s solubility still decides the isolation method.

example.question: Predict the salt and other products when magnesium carbonate reacts with dilute nitric acid, and balance the equation.
steps: MgCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O + CO₂.
The salt is magnesium nitrate.
The other products are water and carbon dioxide; atoms balance on both sides.
example.explanation: The pattern connects the carbonate reaction to the chosen acid and ion charges.

commonMistakes: Calling the gas hydrogen.
Omitting water from the carbonate equation.
Assuming every carbonate–acid reaction continues until every solid disappears.

sections.title: Prepare a soluble salt from an insoluble base
paragraphs: For a suitable soluble salt, select an acid and an insoluble reactant that form the desired ions. In the illustrative copper sulfate method, gently warm dilute sulfuric acid using the supervised method, add small portions of copper(II) oxide while stirring, and allow time for each portion to react. Continued solid remaining after adequate mixing indicates an excess under these conditions.

The excess insoluble base consumes the acid and can then be removed by filtration. The residue contains unreacted solid; the filtrate contains the dissolved salt. Filtration does not remove a dissolved acid or dissolved contaminant, so simply filtering an acid-rich mixture does not make it pure.

Partially evaporate water to concentrate the filtrate, then cool a hot saturated solution to form crystals. Separate the crystals from the remaining solution and dry their surface appropriately. Do not evaporate all the solution to dryness as a universal purification method: dissolved impurities can remain with the product, and hydrated crystals can lose water if overheated.

example.question: Explain why excess CuO is useful but excess sulfuric acid is difficult to remove by the same filtration step.
steps: Unreacted CuO is insoluble and can be trapped by the filter.
Sulfuric acid remains dissolved and passes through with the solution.
The correct excess improves consumption of acid without relying on filtration to remove dissolved species.
example.explanation: The excess must be compatible with the separation method.

commonMistakes: Collecting the first residue as the soluble salt.
Saying filtration removes dissolved acid.
Boiling every salt solution completely dry to obtain pure crystals.

sections.title: Pure, dry hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals
paragraphs: The required practical starts with copper(II) oxide and dilute sulfuric acid: CuO + H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + H₂O. A black excess solid is filtered away; the blue filtrate is concentrated and cooled to crystallize hydrated copper(II) sulfate. Warming helps the slow initial reaction, but boiling acid is not needed and can cause splashing.

Hydrated crystals contain water as part of their crystal structure. In the familiar pentahydrate, CuSO₄·5H₂O, this is different from liquid water clinging to a crystal. A pure, dry hydrated sample has surface liquid removed while retaining the intended water of crystallization.

Separate formed crystals from the mother liquor and blot them with suitable paper or use an appropriate gentle drying method. Direct strong heating can dehydrate the product. Leaving all the mother liquor to evaporate can also deposit soluble impurities that crystallization and separation were meant to leave behind.

Use eye protection and the teacher’s approved handling, heating and waste method. A colour and a dry-looking surface do not alone prove purity or hydration. This site provides an explanation of the laboratory stages; no actual preparation or measured yield is claimed.

example.question: An invented hydrated-crystal sample has 12.0 g crystals plus 0.8 g clinging solution. Explain why weighing it immediately overstates the isolated crystal mass, and why strong heating is not a suitable correction.
steps: Immediate mass is 12.8 g, including unwanted clinging solution.
Removing surface liquid is needed for a meaningful crystal mass.
Strong heating may remove water of crystallization and change the intended product.
example.explanation: Dryness of the surface and absence of structural water are different conditions.

commonMistakes: Calling dry hydrated crystals water-free.
Treating a blue solution as already isolated crystals.
Claiming the invented mass is a performed experiment.

sections.title: Use titration for a soluble acid–alkali salt — Paper 2C
paragraphs: When both acid and alkali are soluble, excess reagent cannot be removed by ordinary filtration. Use a suitable titration to find the reacting volumes for a measured portion, then repeat using those volumes without indicator to make an uncontaminated salt solution. Suitable starting solutions and a clean setup remain necessary.

For sodium chloride, the model reaction is HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O. Indicator helps locate the preliminary end point, but leaving it in the final preparation adds a soluble impurity. A titre measured with an acid or alkali at one concentration cannot simply be reused after changing its concentration.

Concentrate the indicator-free solution by controlled evaporation, allow crystallization by the method suitable for that salt, separate the crystals and dry them appropriately. Sodium chloride has relatively little change in solubility with temperature, so evaporation contributes strongly to its crystallization; cooling is not equally effective for every soluble salt.

The preliminary titration volume should come from reliable repeat results. Avoid calling the final solution pure just because its pH is neutral: unreacted impurities can remain, and the end point has measurement uncertainty.

example.question: Why is “add excess NaOH and filter it off” unsuitable for preparing NaCl from HCl and NaOH?
steps: NaOH is soluble, so ordinary filtration will not remove the dissolved excess.
Find the reacting volumes by titration.
Repeat without indicator before suitable crystallization and drying.
example.explanation: The method is selected from reactant solubility and product isolation.

commonMistakes: Treating a soluble excess as filterable solid.
Keeping indicator in the intended pure product solution.
Applying old titre volumes to new concentrations.

sections.title: Collect an insoluble salt by precipitation — Paper 2C
paragraphs: Choose two soluble compounds whose aqueous ions can form the desired insoluble salt. Mixing the solutions produces a precipitate when the ionic concentrations are sufficient. The other ions generally remain in the solution; the appearance of cloudiness means solid has formed, not that every species has been removed.

For the school isolation method, mix suitable solutions, filter to collect the precipitate, wash the solid with small portions of distilled water to remove soluble material adhering to it, and dry it appropriately. Here the wanted product is the filter residue, unlike the first filtration in a soluble-salt preparation.

Washing trades impurity removal against possible product loss because solubility is finite. Excessive washing, incomplete precipitation, fine particles passing the filter and loss during transfer can reduce recovery. Evaporating the whole unfiltered mixture would deposit soluble by-products as well as the wanted solid.

example.question: An insoluble product forms alongside dissolved sodium nitrate. Explain how filtration and washing have different purposes.
steps: Filtration separates the solid from most of the solution.
Washing removes soluble material in the liquid clinging to the solid.
Drying removes surface liquid; it does not replace either separation step.
example.explanation: The three stages address different parts of product isolation.

commonMistakes: Calling the filtrate the wanted insoluble salt.
Evaporating all the mixture to obtain a pure precipitate.
Assuming washing cannot lose any product.

sections.title: Prepare lead(II) sulfate by precipitation — Paper 2C
paragraphs: For the required school example, lead(II) nitrate solution supplies Pb²⁺ and sodium sulfate solution supplies SO₄²⁻. Their mixture forms white lead(II) sulfate under suitable conditions: Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + Na₂SO₄(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq). Both starting compounds are soluble under the required rules; PbSO₄ is an insoluble sulfate exception.

The net ionic equation is Pb²⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq) → PbSO₄(s), with zero total charge on each side. Nitrate and sodium are spectator ions. Collect the precipitate by filtration, wash with small portions of distilled water and dry using the approved method, avoiding direct heating because the sample may decompose, to obtain the intended pure, dry sample.

Lead compounds are toxic: this required practical belongs in a supervised laboratory using approved handling and separate lead-waste collection, not disposal to a sink. This is a method explanation, not evidence that a sample has been prepared. White appearance alone cannot establish identity or purity; reagent identity and the separation steps are essential.

example.question: Why are lead(II) nitrate and sodium sulfate appropriate soluble starting compounds, while adding solid lead(II) sulfate itself is not a precipitation preparation?
steps: The soluble reagents provide the two needed ions in solution.
Those ions form new PbSO₄ solid when mixed.
Starting with the product does not demonstrate its formation from soluble reactants.
example.explanation: The method explains both the ion sources and the reaction producing the solid.

commonMistakes: Using sulfate and sulfide as interchangeable names.
Writing Pb₂SO₄ instead of charge-neutral PbSO₄.
Treating a white precipitate as proof of purity.

sections.title: Choose the separation method from solubility
paragraphs: Ask first whether the target salt is soluble. For a soluble product and a suitable insoluble base, excess base can be filtered out and crystals obtained from the filtrate. For a soluble product from an acid and alkali, measure the reacting amounts by titration because a soluble excess cannot be filtered out.

For an insoluble product made from two soluble reagents, precipitation is followed by filtration, washing and drying of the residue. “Filter the mixture” is incomplete unless the answer says what is being removed and which fraction contains the wanted product.

This comparison connects requirements that have different paper applicability: the insoluble-base soluble-salt method is on both papers, while the acid–alkali and two-solution precipitation methods are Paper 2C-only. Use the named reactants and the exact required solubility rules before choosing a route.

example.question: Identify the fraction to keep after the first filtration for CuSO₄ made using excess CuO, and for PbSO₄ made by mixing soluble reagents.
steps: CuSO₄ preparation: keep the filtrate; excess CuO is the residue.
PbSO₄ preparation: keep the residue; soluble by-products are in the filtrate.
The desired product’s solubility explains the difference.
example.explanation: The same apparatus can serve opposite product-collection roles.

commonMistakes: Memorizing keep the residue for every filtration.
Ignoring whether excess reagent is soluble.
Treating all compared methods as both-paper requirements.

diagram.alt: Original comparison of three salt-preparation routes: soluble salt from insoluble base keeps the filtrate; acid and alkali use measured volumes; precipitation keeps the residue.
diagram.caption: Choose the route from reactant and product solubility. This is a method comparison, not a record of performed experiments.

sections.title: Distinguish purity, dryness and recovery
paragraphs: Purity describes the absence of unwanted substances; dryness concerns surface liquid; recovery is how much desired product is isolated compared with an appropriate expected amount. A sample can look dry yet contain solid impurities, or be chemically appropriate but still wet.

Some salt remains dissolved in the mother liquor after crystallization. Cooling longer does not guarantee that all dissolved salt crystallizes, and transferring or filtering can lose material. More aggressive evaporation can increase the recovered mass while also bringing soluble impurities into the crystals, so maximum mass is not automatically maximum purity.

Evaluate a method using evidence: identify a likely contaminant, show how a separation removes it, and explain any loss or uncertainty. Compare recovery on the same hydration basis for a hydrated product. No numerical purity, yield or practical success is certified by the descriptions here.

example.question: A proposed method evaporates all the mother liquor because it gives a larger mass. Why does that not establish a better purified product?
steps: The extra solid can include previously dissolved impurities.
Greater measured mass can include unwanted species or liquid.
Purity and useful recovery need separate evidence.
example.explanation: An isolation method has more than one success criterion.

commonMistakes: Equating mass with purity.
Calling a dry surface proof of correct hydration.
Assuming no desired salt remains dissolved.

sections.title: Distinguish hydrogen and oxygen splint tests
paragraphs: For the standard supervised hydrogen test, a lighted splint at the mouth of a small test tube of gas gives a squeaky pop. For oxygen, a glowing splint inserted into the gas relights. Lighted and glowing describe different starting conditions; stating only “use a splint” leaves the test ambiguous.

Hydrogen is combustible, while oxygen supports combustion in the oxygen test. Do not describe oxygen as the gas that burns with a pop. An oxygen-containing sample can make combustion more vigorous without being pure oxygen, so the inference is presence of sufficient oxygen under the test conditions.

A weak or negative result can reflect a small gas amount, dilution with air or an unsuitable splint, as well as absence of the target gas. Use the test specified for the sample and teacher-approved quantities; these explanations are not evidence of a performed gas collection.

example.question: Improve “the gas makes a splint burn” into the two distinct required gas-test observations.
steps: Hydrogen: a lighted splint gives a squeaky pop.
Oxygen: a glowing splint relights.
Name the test condition and the gas separately.
example.explanation: The starting splint condition is part of the evidence.

commonMistakes: Swapping lighted and glowing splints.
Calling oxygen combustible in this test.
Treating no clear pop from a tiny sample as conclusive absence of hydrogen.

sections.title: Carbon dioxide clouds limewater
paragraphs: Bubble the gas through limewater, the clear aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide, using the supervised test setup. Carbon dioxide produces a white calcium carbonate precipitate, making it cloudy or milky. The gas bubbles alone are not the positive observation.

The school equation is CO₂ + Ca(OH)₂ → CaCO₃ + H₂O. A dispersed insoluble solid causes cloudiness; the limewater is not simply dyed white. With enough additional carbon dioxide the precipitate can dissolve into soluble hydrogencarbonate-containing solution, so prolonged bubbling can remove an earlier positive result.

Observe and record the sequence. Clear old limewater or a poorly delivered gas sample can give an unhelpful test; a fresh appropriate reagent and known comparison help evaluate the result. This is an explanation of the standard inference, not a claim that every possible gas mixture has been identified.

example.question: In an invented test, limewater first clouds and later clears during prolonged gas passage. Does the final clear appearance erase the earlier evidence?
steps: No: initial white precipitate is the expected carbon-dioxide evidence.
Further CO₂ can dissolve the precipitate under the stated conditions.
Record the sequence rather than only the final appearance.
example.explanation: An observation can change as further reaction occurs.

commonMistakes: Calling bubbling itself the CO₂ test result.
Calling a white solution a precipitate without solid formation.
Ignoring an earlier positive observation.

sections.title: Damp litmus distinguishes ammonia and chlorine
paragraphs: Ammonia gas turns damp red litmus paper blue because it gives an alkaline solution in the moisture on the paper. Dampness matters: the gas must interact with water for this acid–base response. Keep the paper out of direct contact with an alkaline reaction mixture, which could turn it blue without showing an evolved gas.

Chlorine bleaches damp litmus paper white. Damp blue litmus may first turn red before bleaching; the lasting white/bleached result is the key chlorine observation. Red alone indicates an acidic response and is insufficient to establish the bleaching test.

Chlorine gas and chloride ions are different species and have different tests. A chloride solution is tested with acidified silver nitrate, not by expecting it to bleach litmus. Ammonia and chlorine are irritating gases; use the teacher-approved sample and ventilation, and do not use direct smelling as the identification method.

example.question: An invented chloride-salt solution is tested with damp blue litmus because a student remembers chlorine’s test. Correct the species and method.
steps: The target is Cl⁻ ions in solution, not Cl₂ gas.
Use dilute nitric acid followed by silver nitrate solution.
A white precipitate supports chloride; chlorine’s damp-litmus bleaching is a different test.
example.explanation: Species identity determines which evidence is relevant.

commonMistakes: Calling chloride and chlorine interchangeable.
Reporting red litmus alone as chlorine bleaching.
Testing litmus by dipping it into NaOH when the intended evidence is ammonia gas.

sections.title: Carry out a clean flame test
paragraphs: In one school method, use a clean nichrome wire loop to introduce a small sample into the edge of a non-luminous blue Bunsen flame and observe the colour. The teacher’s specified cleaning method may use dilute hydrochloric acid and heating until the clean loop adds no characteristic colour. A cleaned loop is checked before testing another sample.

Alternative approved methods use separate soaked wooden splints. The apparatus choice can differ while the purpose remains the same: compare the sample’s characteristic flame colour with known results under similar conditions. Do not confuse the colour of an unheated salt or solution with its flame-test colour.

Contamination can dominate the result. In particular, sodium gives a strong yellow emission that can mask weaker colours, so a yellow result from a contaminated loop is not secure evidence about an unknown alone. Record uncertainty, use clean apparatus and follow the supervised heat and eye-protection procedure; no flame test has been performed by this site.

example.question: A clean loop gives no characteristic colour, but a loop reused after sodium gives yellow with an unknown. What should be checked before identifying the unknown?
steps: Clean the loop using the specified method and verify a blank response.
Test a fresh sample under comparable conditions.
Consider sodium contamination before concluding that the unknown contains sodium.
example.explanation: A control helps separate apparatus contamination from sample evidence.

commonMistakes: Using a bright luminous flame that obscures the sample colour.
Reusing contaminated wire without checking it.
Identifying a cation from the unheated solution’s colour.

sections.title: The five required cation flame colours
paragraphs: The required reference colours are Li⁺: red; Na⁺: yellow; K⁺: lilac; Ca²⁺: orange-red; Cu²⁺: blue-green. Use Pearson’s labels when recalling this five-cation set. A visible shade can vary with sample, conditions and the observer, so a screen illustration is not a calibrated spectrum.

The cation associated with the sample is what this school test helps identify; it does not establish the accompanying anion. A sodium chloride sample and another suitable sodium salt can both give the sodium flame colour. Copper’s blue-green flame is not the same observation as its blue hydroxide precipitate.

A mixture can show a dominant or blended response. Sodium masking and similar red tones can make a single colour less decisive. Combine the result with the context or further appropriate evidence rather than assuming a perfectly pure single salt.

example.question: An invented salt gives a lilac flame under clean conditions. Which required cation is supported, and has its anion been identified?
steps: Potassium, K⁺, is supported by lilac.
The flame result does not identify the anion.
Other suitable evidence is needed to name the full salt.
example.explanation: Cation evidence is only part of a compound identification.

commonMistakes: Calling the lilac result lithium.
Inferring chloride automatically from a flame colour.
Equating a flame colour with a precipitation colour.

sections.title: NaOH precipitates identify three metal cations
paragraphs: Add sodium hydroxide solution to a separate aqueous sample, initially dropwise, and describe the solid formed. Cu²⁺ gives a blue copper(II) hydroxide precipitate; Fe²⁺ gives a green iron(II) hydroxide precipitate; Fe³⁺ gives a brown or red-brown iron(III) hydroxide precipitate. These three remain insoluble in excess NaOH in the school comparison.

The illustrative ionic equations are Cu²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Cu(OH)₂, Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂ and Fe³⁺ + 3OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₃. Each has zero total charge on the left and a neutral solid on the right. Say “blue precipitate” rather than just “blue colour”, since the initial solution may already be coloured.

The green iron(II) precipitate can turn brown as it is oxidized on exposure to air. Record its initial appearance promptly and describe any later change. An old brown sample cannot be identified as originally Fe³⁺ solely from its final colour; mixtures, insufficient reagent and very dilute samples can also limit the inference.

example.question: An invented sample gives a green precipitate immediately with NaOH and becomes brown on standing. Which initial ion is supported?
steps: Initial green precipitate supports Fe²⁺.
Later brown appearance is consistent with oxidation of the iron(II) product.
The time sequence matters; final brown alone is not the whole evidence.
example.explanation: The test describes both a solid and its changing state.

commonMistakes: Writing Fe(OH)₂ for the iron(III) product.
Calling a blue solution the required blue precipitate observation.
Ignoring oxidation while leaving an iron(II) test to stand.

sections.title: Warm with NaOH and test for evolved ammonia
paragraphs: For NH₄⁺, add sodium hydroxide solution and warm gently using the approved school method. Ammonia is evolved and turns damp red litmus paper blue when tested in the gas above the mixture. Bubbles or a smell alone are not the complete identification.

The net ionic equation is NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ → NH₃ + H₂O. Nitrogen is conserved, the five hydrogen atoms on the left appear as three in NH₃ plus two in water, and charge +1 − 1 = 0 matches the neutral products.

Use a separate fresh sample and keep the litmus away from alkaline liquid or spray. Direct contact with NaOH could mimic the blue response without proving NH₄⁺. Warming aids gas release; it does not transform the nitrate test into an ammonium test unless the intended reagents and reaction are specified.

example.question: Why must damp red litmus be tested in the gas, rather than dipped into the NaOH-containing mixture?
steps: NaOH itself is alkaline and can turn the paper blue.
The required observation concerns evolved ammonia gas.
Avoiding liquid contact helps rule out that false explanation.
example.explanation: The location of the test is part of its validity.

commonMistakes: Writing NH₃⁺ for ammonium.
Using bubbles alone to identify ammonia.
Testing a reagent’s alkalinity instead of the evolved gas.

sections.title: Acidified silver nitrate distinguishes halides
paragraphs: Use a separate aqueous sample, acidify with dilute nitric acid, then add silver nitrate solution. Chloride gives white AgCl precipitate, bromide gives cream AgBr and iodide gives yellow AgI. Describe a precipitate, not simply the solution becoming a colour.

The ionic pattern is Ag⁺ + X⁻ → AgX(s), where X⁻ is the named halide ion. Acidification removes interfering carbonate under the school test conditions. Hydrochloric acid is unsuitable for this preparation because it introduces chloride and can create a false AgCl result.

Use fresh separate portions for different anion tests. A sample previously treated with HCl in the carbonate or sulfate test has been supplied with chloride, even if it originally contained none. The colours support the named ions in the appropriate comparison, but mixtures or contamination can obscure them; additional ammonia-solubility tests are extensions rather than an added requirement here.

example.question: A sample treated with HCl is later used for an AgNO₃ test and gives white solid. Why is this not secure proof of chloride in the original sample?
steps: The HCl treatment introduced Cl⁻.
Added Ag⁺ can form AgCl from that introduced chloride.
Use a fresh portion acidified with dilute nitric acid for the intended halide test.
example.explanation: A reagent can introduce the species that the next test is supposed to identify.

commonMistakes: Using chlorine’s litmus test for chloride ions.
Using hydrochloric acid to acidify the halide-test sample.
Writing AgCl₂ for the silver chloride precipitate.

sections.title: Acidified barium chloride tests for sulfate
paragraphs: For sulfate, acidify a separate aqueous portion with dilute hydrochloric acid, then add barium chloride solution. A white barium sulfate precipitate supports sulfate: Ba²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → BaSO₄(s). Total charge is zero and the one-to-one ion ratio gives the neutral solid.

The acid helps remove carbonate that could otherwise give a white barium carbonate precipitate. Do not use sulfuric acid for acidification: it would supply the sulfate being tested for and can give a misleading positive result.

White precipitate is the expected observation with the appropriate reagents and preparation. It is not a universal identity for every white solid. Keep the sulfate test separate from the silver-nitrate test, and use approved handling and waste procedures because soluble barium reagents are hazardous.

example.question: Explain why HCl is useful for this sulfate test while H₂SO₄ would undermine the inference.
steps: HCl acidifies without introducing sulfate.
Acid helps remove carbonate interference.
H₂SO₄ introduces SO₄²⁻ and can itself cause BaSO₄ precipitation.
example.explanation: The acid’s ions matter, not merely whether it is acidic.

commonMistakes: Using sulfuric acid to prove sulfate was originally present.
Calling a white precipitate uniquely barium sulfate without naming reagents.
Forgetting acidification and carbonate interference.

sections.title: Acid release plus gas identification tests for carbonate
paragraphs: Add dilute hydrochloric acid to a separate sample. A carbonate releases carbon dioxide; confirm the evolved gas by its clouding of limewater. Effervescence followed by the appropriate gas-test result supplies stronger evidence than reporting bubbles alone.

The net reaction is CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → CO₂ + H₂O. Carbon1, oxygen3 and hydrogen2 are conserved, and the left charge −2 + 2 = 0 matches the neutral products. The limewater test is a second reaction forming a precipitate.

Keep the two observations separate: gas release in the original sample, then white cloudiness in limewater. A reactive metal can also bubble with acid, but its hydrogen does not give the same carbonate/CO₂ evidence. Some other substances can also release CO₂, so apply the inference within the stated school sample context.

example.question: An invented sample bubbles after HCl addition. What further required observation supports carbonate rather than merely proving gas release?
steps: Pass the evolved gas into limewater using the approved setup.
White cloudiness is consistent with CO₂.
Combine that with the acid reaction and the given sample context.
example.explanation: The gas must be identified rather than assumed from effervescence.

commonMistakes: Calling every acid-generated gas CO₂.
Saying the original sample must turn limewater-white itself.
Omitting the second observation.

sections.title: Anhydrous copper sulfate shows water is present
paragraphs: White anhydrous copper(II) sulfate becomes blue when it takes up water and forms hydrated material. Use the teacher’s specified test with a small fresh sample of the reagent. The required evidence is the white-to-blue change, rather than the presence of blue copper sulfate before the test starts.

The test establishes water presence in a suitable sample; it does not show that the sample is pure water. A solution containing water and dissolved salt can still give the positive response. Water from damp apparatus or atmospheric moisture can also compromise a blank test.

The distinction matches the salt-preparation lesson: hydrated crystals contain structural water, while anhydrous material lacks that hydration. Avoid relying on direct strong heating of an unknown as the identification method; the named reagent and observed change are the requirement here.

example.question: A mixture of water and dissolved salt turns fresh white anhydrous CuSO₄ blue. Does this prove the mixture is chemically pure water?
steps: No: the test supports water being present.
Dissolved substances may also be present.
A different physical purity check is needed for the next requirement.
example.explanation: Presence and purity are different questions.

commonMistakes: Starting with blue hydrated reagent and calling no change a positive test.
Calling any positive hydration test proof of purity.
Ignoring water already on the apparatus.

sections.title: Compare a phase-change temperature with pure water
paragraphs: A physical school test compares a measured phase-change temperature with the reference for pure water at the same pressure. At standard atmospheric pressure, pure water boils at about 100°C and melts/freezes at about 0°C. A sharp phase-change temperature consistent with the appropriate reference supports purity in the school comparison.

Pressure matters especially for boiling point: a lower atmospheric pressure can make pure water boil below 100°C. Dissolved substances can change a freezing or boiling point, but a measured deviation is not automatically proof of one particular impurity; thermometer calibration, heating method and pressure also need consideration.

In an approved boiling-point method, measure the liquid’s temperature when it is steadily boiling, using correctly positioned suitable apparatus rather than touching the heater or vessel wall. Compare with a reference measured under comparable conditions. A result within the measurement resolution cannot exclude every trace impurity.

The water-presence chemical test, clear appearance and a phase-change test answer different questions. None of these alone certifies that an unknown is safe to drink. No sample or phase-change curve has actually been measured here.

example.question: An invented sample boils at 98°C. Before calling it impure solely because it differs from 100°C, name two checks.
steps: Check atmospheric pressure against the reference conditions.
Check the thermometer and its measurement position/calibration.
Then interpret the result within the experiment’s resolution and other evidence.
example.explanation: A physical reference is meaningful only with appropriate conditions.

commonMistakes: Assuming pure water boils at 100°C at every pressure.
Using white-to-blue CuSO₄ as proof of purity.
Claiming one approximate result excludes every trace contaminant.

sections.title: Separate the test, observation and conclusion
paragraphs: A useful answer names the test condition, records a concrete observation and then identifies what it supports. “Add NaOH; a blue precipitate forms; Cu²⁺ is supported” is more complete than “it turns blue”. A precipitate is a solid, while a flame colour, a gas response and a solution colour are different observations.

Plan separate fresh portions when reagents can interfere with later tests. HCl used in a carbonate test supplies chloride; sulfuric acid supplies sulfate. Controls and clean apparatus help establish that the expected response belongs to the sample rather than a reagent or contamination.

Do not claim a whole compound’s identity from one ion test. Combining an appropriate cation test and an appropriate anion test can narrow the proposed salt, while mixtures and other possibilities still need the context. Negative results have detection and reagent limitations; report the evidence rather than inventing a definitive purity claim.

example.question: A proposed salt gives a blue precipitate with NaOH and, in a fresh properly acidified portion, a white precipitate with barium chloride. What named ions are supported?
steps: Cu²⁺ is supported by the NaOH blue precipitate.
SO₄²⁻ is supported by the acidified barium test.
Copper(II) sulfate is consistent with those ions in a single-salt context; the observations do not prove every purity condition.
example.explanation: Separate tests combine compatible evidence without exceeding it.

commonMistakes: Calling a white precipitate enough to identify the whole compound.
Reusing a contaminated sample for another ion test.
Claiming a negative result proves absolute absence at any concentration.
